blocks.h: 1. (a) The three principles the LLMC regime is built on

blocks.p: The Convention on Limitation of Liability for Maritime Claims, 1976 was adopted on 19 November 1976 and entered into force on 1 December 1986. It rests on three organising ideas.

ol: A right to limit that is, in practice, unbreakable. Article 1 gives it to shipowners, charterers, managers and operators, to salvors, to those for whose acts they answer, and to their insurers. Article 4 removes it only for that person's personal act or omission, committed with intent to cause such loss, or recklessly and with knowledge that such loss would probably result. Because the fault must be personal, negligent navigation by the master does not break it.

The limit is fixed by tonnage, not by fault or by the size of the loss. Article 6 computes a global amount from gross tonnage, with a higher tranche for loss of life and personal injury than for property; Article 7 deals separately with passenger claims.

One fund per occurrence, distributed rateably. Articles 11 to 13 allow a single limitation fund; claimants are confined to it and rank rateably, and other assets are protected from arrest for those claims.

blocks.h: 2. How LLMC links to the other liability conventions

blocks.p: LLMC is the general, residual regime, and the specialised conventions relate to it in two opposite ways.

ul: Conventions with their own limits stand outside it. The CLC 1992 creates strict, channelled liability on the registered owner for tanker oil pollution, with its own limits, compulsory insurance and direct action. LLMC therefore expressly excepts CLC oil pollution claims at Article 3.

Conventions with no limits of their own borrow LLMC's. The Bunkers Convention 2001 imposes strict liability but sets no limits; Article 6 preserves the right to limit under the applicable regime, in practice LLMC. The Nairobi Wreck Removal Convention 2007 does the same at Article 10(2).
So a bunker spill and a wreck removal limit in the LLMC fund; a tanker cargo spill under CLC. States may, however, reserve against LLMC applying to wreck removal.

blocks.h: 3. (b) The liabilities that are subject to limitation

blocks.p: Article 2 lists the limitable claims, whatever the basis of liability may be:

ul: loss of life or personal injury and loss of or damage to property occurring on board or in direct connexion with the operation of the ship or with salvage operations, including consequential loss;
loss from delay in the carriage of cargo, passengers or luggage;
loss from infringement of rights other than contractual rights in direct connexion with those operations;
raising, removal, destruction or rendering harmless of a wrecked or sunken ship and its cargo, subject to reservation;
claims by a person other than the person liable for measures taken to avert or minimise loss.

blocks.h: 4. The claims left outside, and the conduct that breaks the limit

ul: Article 3 excepts salvage and contribution in general average - a salvor's earned award cannot itself be cut down by the regime;
CLC oil pollution damage and nuclear damage, each having its own regime;
claims by servants of the shipowner or salvor, where the law governing the contract of service does not permit limitation;
and the limit falls away under Article 4 on proof of personal intentional or reckless conduct - a burden on the claimant, very rarely discharged.

blocks.h: 5. (c) The principles of the Salvage Convention 1989

blocks.p: The International Convention on Salvage, 1989 was adopted on 28 April 1989 and entered into force on 14 July 1996, replacing the Brussels Convention of 1910:

ul: salvage is a voluntary service to property in danger, outside any pre-existing duty, and no cure, no pay is the base rule - a reward is earned only by a useful result;

the reward is fixed on the Article 13 criteria - salved value, skill and efforts in preventing environmental damage, success, danger, time and expenses, risk of liability, promptness, availability of craft - and may not exceed the salved value;

Article 14 special compensation corrects the 1910 blind spot: where the vessel threatened environmental damage and the salvor earned no reward or a lesser one, the owner pays his expenses plus up to 30% where such damage was minimised or prevented, raisable to 100% of expenses if fair and just;

Article 8 imposes duties both ways - due care and best endeavours to prevent environmental damage on the salvor, full co-operation on owner and master - and commercially it is worked through Lloyd's Open Form, with SCOPIC as a tariff-rate alternative to assessing Article 14.

blocks.h: 6. Why salvors may limit, and the limit that applies

blocks.p: The rationale is a specific failure of the previous regime. In The Tojo Maru a salvage company's diver, working in the water and not on board the salvage tug, negligently caused an explosion in the casualty. Under the 1957 Convention a salvor could limit only when operating from a vessel and where the act was done on board or in her navigation or management; the diver's act was neither, so the salvor faced unlimited liability.

LLMC 1976 answered it directly. Article 1 makes salvors persons entitled to limit, and Article 1(3) defines a salvor broadly as any person rendering services in direct connexion with salvage operations - covering the diver in the water. Because such a salvor may have no ship, Article 6(4) supplies a notional figure: limits calculated according to a tonnage of 1,500 tons.

That deemed tonnage falls in the lowest band, not exceeding 2,000 gross tonnage. In a State party to the 1996 Protocol as amended by the 2012 amendments, in force 8 June 2015, the limits are 3.02 million SDR for loss of life or personal injury and 1.51 million SDR for property claims. A State bound only by the unamended 1976 Convention applies lower figures, so the instrument must be identified before quoting any figure. India is a party through Part XA of the Merchant Shipping Act 1958, the 1996 Protocol and its 2012 amendments being given effect by rules made in 2015 and 2017.

blocks.h: Why this structure scores

blocks.p: The paper prints 5 + 5 + 6 and the route puts two headings under each limb, so an examiner marking limb by limb can see all three answered without hunting. The commonest way to lose marks here is to write everything you know about LLMC and never reach limb (c), which carries the most marks and the only question that needs a number.

blocks.h: Limitation is not insurance, and not a compensation fund

blocks.p: The convention family divides into liability instruments, which say who pays and on what basis; compensation instruments, which provide a fund that actually pays claimants, such as the IOPC Funds; and limitation instruments, which cap exposure. LLMC is purely the third. It creates no cause of action, provides no money and protects no claimant - it protects the defendant. The limitation fund is money the shipowner puts up out of his own pocket or his P&I cover, not a pooled international fund. Candidates who describe LLMC as "the fund that compensates victims" have confused it with the IOPC Fund Convention.

blocks.h: Why the limit is almost never broken

blocks.p: Article 4 looks like a normal fault test but is not. Three things narrow it almost to vanishing: the act must be the liable person's own, so vicarious fault does not count; the state of mind must be intent or recklessness with knowledge that such loss would probably result, which is far above gross negligence; and the burden lies on the claimant. In a corporate owner the search is for the directing mind, which is why the limit survives most casualties. This is deliberate policy: predictable exposure is what makes marine liability insurable at all, and an insurable industry is what allows claimants to be paid.

blocks.h: Common mistakes

ul: Treating LLMC as a compensation convention, or confusing the limitation fund with the IOPC Funds.
Saying the limit is broken by "negligence" or by "the master's recklessness" - Article 4 requires the liable person's personal conduct.
Trying to limit a salvage award or a general average contribution. Article 3 excepts both.
Quoting a salvor's limit as a fixed sum without explaining the deemed 1,500 tons, or without saying which instrument the State has accepted.
Answering limb (c) on salvage only and never reaching the limitation half, which is where the marks concentrate.
Citing the Salvage Convention as though it displaced Lloyd's Open Form. It underlies LOF; it does not replace contractual salvage.

blocks.h: Examiner traps

ul: "Its linkage with two other IMO Liability and compensation Conventions" - naming two conventions scores little. The mark is in the relationship: one excludes LLMC, the other borrows it.
"The current liability limit applicable to them" - the word current is doing work. It asks for the post-2012 figures, not the 1976 originals.
The three principles are not a printed list anywhere. Any defensible three anchored to articles will score; three unsupported slogans will not.

blocks.h: Likely oral follow-up

ul: What is an SDR and why are limits expressed in it?
Your ship's bunker tank ruptures alongside and oils a marina. Which convention governs, and where do you find the limit?
A salvor damages your main engine while refloating you. Can he limit? Against what tonnage?
Can a claimant arrest a sister ship after a limitation fund has been constituted?
Does India apply the 1996 Protocol limits?

blocks.h: Memory framework

blocks.p: Three principles as WHO - HOW MUCH - ONE POT. The linkage as OUT (CLC) and IN (Bunkers, Nairobi). Limb (b) as IN then OUT. Limb (c) as EARN then LIMIT. The single number chain: 1,500 deemed tons, so the under-2,000 band, so 3.02 and 1.51 million SDR.

blocks.h: Regulation and source map

ul: LLMC 1976 - Art 1 persons entitled; Art 1(3) salvor; Art 2 claims subject; Art 3 excepted; Art 4 conduct barring; Art 6 general limits and Art 6(4) salvors; Art 7 passengers; Arts 11-13 the fund.
LLMC 1996 Protocol, as amended by the 2012 amendments adopted 19 April 2012, in force 8 June 2015.
Salvage Convention 1989 - Art 8 duties, Art 12 no cure no pay, Art 13 reward criteria, Art 14 special compensation.
Bunkers Convention 2001 Art 6; Nairobi WRC 2007 Art 10(2); CLC 1992.
India - Merchant Shipping Act 1958 Part XA, with the 1996 Protocol and 2012 amendments given effect by rules of 2015 and 2017.

blocks.h: Uncertainty, jurisdiction and currency

blocks.p: The limit figures are those of the 1996 Protocol as amended in 2012 and apply only in States bound by it; a State party only to the unamended 1976 Convention applies lower figures. The Protocol carries a tacit acceptance procedure for raising the amounts, so the figures are inherently perishable and are flagged for a currency check before being relied on. India's implementation is through Part XA of the Merchant Shipping Act 1958 with modifications; commentary records that the Indian text departs from the Convention in places, and MIW has not read Part XA in the statute, so the answer states the Convention position and flags the Indian variation rather than asserting its content. Note also that the Merchant Shipping Act 2025 repealed the 1958 Act with effect from 15 March 2026 - after this sitting, but before any publication of this answer.

Salvors were given the right to limit because The Tojo Maru showed a salvor working off his own tug could not limit at all. questions.understand_first: Limiting liability is not the same as insuring against it, and the two are constantly confused. LLMC does not pay anybody; it caps what a claimant can recover from the shipowner or salvor, whatever the true size of the loss, and it does so by reference to the ship's tonnage rather than to who was at fault. Read the convention family as a division of labour: CLC and the other pollution conventions carry their own limits and compulsory insurance, so LLMC stands out of their way; conventions such as Bunkers and Nairobi create liability but no limits of their own and simply borrow LLMC's.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What is the difference between the way CLC 1992 and the Bunkers Convention 2001 deal with limitation?
retrieval_cards.answer: CLC carries its own limits and its own compulsory insurance, and LLMC expressly does not apply to claims within it. Bunkers creates liability but no limits of its own; Article 6 preserves the right to limit under the applicable regime, which is normally LLMC.
retrieval_cards.why: This is the linkage the examiner is asking for, and it is the difference between a self-contained regime and a borrowed one.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Which claims does LLMC 1976 except from limitation?
retrieval_cards.answer: Claims for salvage and for contribution in general average; claims for oil pollution damage within the CLC; nuclear damage claims; and claims by the shipowner's or salvor's own servants.
retrieval_cards.why: Article 3. Candidates routinely try to limit a salvage award, which is precisely what the Convention forbids.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What conduct breaks the right to limit under LLMC 1976, and whose conduct must it be?
retrieval_cards.answer: The person's own personal act or omission, committed with intent to cause such loss, or recklessly and with knowledge that such loss would probably result. It must be personal, so the negligence of the master or crew does not break it.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What is special compensation under the Salvage Convention 1989, and why does it exist?
retrieval_cards.answer: Where a salvor works on a ship threatening damage to the environment and earns no reward, or a reward less than the special compensation, the owner must pay the salvor's expenses, plus up to 30% where environmental damage was minimised or prevented, which a tribunal may raise to up to 100% of expenses if fair and just.

retrieval_cards.answer: Because The Tojo Maru showed the gap: under the 1957 regime a salvor could limit only when operating from a vessel and acting on board or in its navigation or management, so a diver working in the water off the tug left the salvor with unlimited exposure.

blocks.h: 1. a) What CII is, and where it sits in MARPOL

blocks.p: The Carbon Intensity Indicator is the operational half of the IMO's short-term GHG measure, imposed by MARPOL Annex VI regulation 28, 'Operational carbon intensity'. It applies to ships of 5,000 gross tonnage and above - the threshold of the IMO Data Collection System under regulation 27, on whose fuel data it runs. It must be distinguished from EEXI, a one-off design index applying from 400 gt: EEXI asks what the ship is capable of, CII what she actually did last year.

blocks.h: 2. How attained and required CII are set, and how a ship is rated

ul: The ship calculates an attained annual operational CII - CO2 per unit of transport work over the calendar year. For most cargo ship types this is the AER, CO2 divided by deadweight capacity multiplied by distance sailed; cruise and ro-pax types use a different metric.

The required annual operational CII is the 2019 reference line for that ship type and size reduced by a factor Z: required CII = reference value x (1 - Z/100). Z is 5% for 2023, 7% for 2024, 9% for 2025 and 11% for 2026, extended by resolution MEPC.400(83) to 13.625%, 16.250%, 18.875% and 21.500% for 2027 to 2030.
The attained value is verified annually and the ship rated A to E, C being the required standard, the rating recorded with the Statement of Compliance issued under the DCS.
The factors were set so that, with the rest of Annex VI, shipping reduces CO2 per transport work by at least 40% by 2030 compared with 2008.

blocks.h: 3. What follows from a poor rating

blocks.p: There is no fine and no detention. The consequence is administrative: a ship rated D for three consecutive years, or E for one year, must develop a corrective action plan showing how the required index of C or above will be achieved. It is incorporated in SEEMP Part III and agreed before the Statement of Compliance is issued, so a ship that ignores it cannot keep her documentation in order. Incentives to A- and B-rated ships are encouraged.

blocks.h: 4. The commercial impact on the shipping business

blocks.p: The commercial effect far exceeds the regulatory sanction, because the rating is a public, comparable letter grade on an asset:

ul: Chartering. Charterers screen tonnage on rating and some will not fix D or E ships. Because a time charterer controls speed and routing - the very things that set the rating - CII clauses are now standard, notably the BIMCO CII Operations Clause 2022. Who bears a bad rating is a negotiated term.

Operational control shifts. Owners reserve rights over speed, hull and propeller cleaning and voyage optimisation, so slow steaming becomes contractual - with the machinery consequences of prolonged low-load running that follow.
Finance. Lenders under the Poseidon Principles report portfolio climate alignment, so rating feeds into the cost and availability of debt.
Asset value. A persistent D or E shortens commercial life, depresses second-hand values and brings forward retrofit or scrapping decisions.
Cargo owners. Shippers reporting their own scope 3 emissions demand rating data, so pressure comes from the cargo side too.

blocks.h: 5. b) The shortcomings the industry has identified

ul: It rewards capacity, not cargo. The AER denominator is deadweight capacity times distance, not cargo carried, so a ship can improve her rating by sailing further with less on board while absolute emissions rise - a genuine perverse incentive.

Waiting is punished, sailing is not. Idling at anchor adds fuel but no distance. Port congestion and 'sail fast then wait' lie outside the ship's control, and the incentive to keep moving can increase emissions.

Trade patterns are penalised structurally. Short-sea, multi-parcel chemical and product, offshore and ice-class vessels and ships with long port stays are disadvantaged by a metric built around long laden passages, however efficiently run.
Responsibility and control are split. The rating attaches to the ship and the owner's documentation, but a time charterer determines speed, route, waiting and cargo intake.
It is an efficiency ratio used as a climate instrument. Being indexed rather than absolute, improving average CII does not itself guarantee a fall in total emissions.

blocks.h: 6. The remedial measures actually adopted

blocks.p: The regulation anticipated this. Regulation 28.11 required a review of the CII requirements to be completed by 1 January 2026, covering effectiveness, reinforced corrective action, enforcement, the data collection system and revision of the Z factor and reference values.

ul: Phase 1 was completed at MEPC 83 in April 2025: implementation experience was gathered and analysed and a list of challenges and gaps identified.
Resolution MEPC.400(83), adopted 11 April 2025, amended the G3 Guidelines to set the 2027 to 2030 reduction factors, aligned with the 2023 GHG Strategy's carbon-intensity ambition.
The SEEMP Guidelines were also amended to allow other CII metrics to be developed at future sessions - the door through which a cargo-based metric would have to come.

Phase 2 opened on 1 January 2026 through intersessional and correspondence groups, addressing the SEEMP framework, further CII metrics and synergies with the IMO Net-Zero Framework. The work plan annexed to the MEPC 83 report runs it through MEPC 84 (spring 2026), MEPC 85 (autumn 2026) and MEPC 86 (spring 2027), and finalizes phase 2 at MEPC 87 in spring 2028, at which revised reference lines and any CII correction factors are also to be settled.
The industry's own remedies have been contractual - the BIMCO clause - and operational, through just-in-time and virtual arrival schemes aimed at waiting time.

blocks.p: As at this sitting the honest position is that the shortcomings were formally acknowledged and the review was under way but not complete: the factors had been extended to 2030, but the metric itself - the source of most criticism - remained under examination in Phase 2.

blocks.h: Why this structure scores

blocks.p: Limb (a) carries 10 of 16 marks and two-thirds of candidates spend it all on the formula. The four steps force the answer up the ladder from instrument to money, and the commercial half is where the differentiating marks are. Limb (b) is short and is best answered as mechanism-then-remedy, because a list of complaints without the mechanism that causes them reads as grumbling rather than analysis.

blocks.h: Why an indexed measure behaves this way

blocks.p: Any ratio can be improved by growing the denominator instead of shrinking the numerator. CII's denominator is transport work, and transport work was defined using deadweight capacity because capacity is a known, verifiable number that appears on every certificate, whereas cargo actually carried is commercially sensitive, unevenly recorded and open to manipulation. The choice was made for auditability, and the perverse incentives are the price of that choice. This is worth understanding rather than memorising, because it explains why the fix is hard: a cargo-based metric would need a trustworthy, global, verifiable source of cargo data that does not currently exist.

blocks.h: CII, EEXI, EEDI and the Net-Zero Framework - keeping them apart

ul: EEDI - design index, new ships, regulation 22. What the ship was built to do.
EEXI - design index applied retrospectively to existing ships from 400 gt, regulation 23. A one-off calculation, often satisfied by engine or shaft power limitation.
CII - operational, annual, ships of 5,000 GT and above, regulation 28. What she actually did.

The Net-Zero Framework - the proposed new Chapter 5, a fuel-intensity standard with a pricing mechanism, which as at this sitting was approved but not adopted. See Q8 of this paper. CII is in force and enforceable; the Net-Zero Framework was not.

blocks.h: Common mistakes

ul: Calling CII a cap on emissions or an emissions trading scheme. It is neither.
Saying a D or E rating attracts a fine or detention. The consequence is a corrective action plan in SEEMP Part III.
Saying 'CII is the AER'. AER is the metric for most cargo ships; cruise and ro-pax use a different one.
Quoting a reduction factor without its year - the figure changes annually and a bare percentage is unmarkable.
Answering limb (b) with what the industry has asked for rather than what was adopted.
Confusing the 5,000 GT CII threshold with the 400 gt EEXI threshold.

blocks.h: Examiner traps

ul: 'As adopted in MARPOL' - the examiner wants the regulation, not a general essay on carbon intensity.
'Commercial impact in shipping business' is half the limb by weight. An answer with no charterparty, finance or asset-value content cannot reach the top band.
'Remedial measures adopted' - the trap is to describe INTERCARGO and ICS submissions as though they were remedies. Name MEPC.400(83) and the two review phases.

blocks.h: Likely oral follow-up

ul: Your ship is heading for a D rating in November. What can you actually do before 31 December?
Who pays if a time charterer's instructions push the ship to an E?
Why does waiting at anchor hurt the rating when the main engine is stopped?
What is in SEEMP Part III that is not in Parts I and II?
Does an A rating relieve you of anything?

blocks.h: Memory framework

blocks.p: Limb (a) as a ladder - INSTRUMENT, MEASURE, CONSEQUENCE, MONEY. Limb (b) as FAULTS then FIXES. One sentence carries the whole critique: capacity not cargo, so distance flatters the rating. One chain carries the remedy: reg 28.11 review - Phase 1 at MEPC 83 - MEPC.400(83) - Phase 2 from 1 January 2026.

blocks.h: Regulation and source map

ul: MARPOL Annex VI reg 28 operational carbon intensity; reg 28.11 the review clause; reg 27 IMO DCS; reg 26 SEEMP.
MEPC.336(76) G1 calculation methods; MEPC.337(76) G2 reference lines; MEPC.338(76) G3 reduction factors; MEPC.339(76) G4 rating.

blocks.h: Uncertainty and currency

blocks.p: This is the most date-sensitive question in the paper after Q8. The reduction factors change every year, the 2027 to 2030 values were only set in April 2025, and Phase 2 of the regulation 28.11 review - which expressly covers revision of the Z factor and the reference lines, and therefore the possibility of a changed metric - opened on 1 January 2026, weeks before this sitting. Every figure here is stated with its year for that reason, and the factors are flagged for a currency check before being relied on. MIW holds no licensed consolidated MARPOL Annex VI, so regulation 28 is cited from the IMO's explanatory material and from the operative text of MEPC.338(76), which quotes regulation 28.11 directly, rather than from the Annex itself. Resolution MEPC.400(83) was not read in full text; its number, date and factors come from the MEPC 83 outcome and consistent class-society summaries.

questions.understand_first: CII does not measure how much a ship emits. It measures how much she emits per unit of transport work, and for most ship types the work is taken as deadweight capacity multiplied by distance sailed - not cargo actually carried. Almost everything the industry complains about follows from that one design choice, because a ship can improve her rating by sailing further with less on board while her absolute emissions rise. Hold that idea and both limbs of this question answer themselves: limb (a) is the machinery of an efficiency ratio, and limb (b) is what happens when an efficiency ratio is used as though it were an emissions cap.

retrieval_cards.answer: Because for most cargo ships the attained CII is the AER, which divides CO2 by deadweight capacity multiplied by distance sailed rather than by cargo actually carried, so extra distance increases the denominator whether or not any cargo moves.
retrieval_cards.why: This is the single most cited shortcoming and it explains most of the others.

blocks.h: 1. a) What FSA is, and who it is for

blocks.p: Formal Safety Assessment is set out in MSC-MEPC.2/Circ.12/Rev.2, Revised Guidelines for Formal Safety Assessment (FSA) for use in the IMO rule-making process, of 9 April 2018. The title states its purpose: a structured, auditable methodology by which the Organization decides whether, and how, to regulate a hazard, balancing safety benefit against cost. It is not a shipboard risk assessment or a permit-to-work system. The question is therefore how a proportionate rule for this cargo was, and is being, arrived at.

blocks.h: 2. Step 1 - identifying the hazards of this cargo

ul: Thermal runaway - an exothermic internal reaction that becomes self-sustaining and generates its own oxidant, so it cannot be smothered and continues without external air;
propagation cell to cell and module to module, and thence vehicle to vehicle in a close stow;
initiators - internal cell defects, mechanical damage in handling or lashing, over-charge, high state of charge on shipment, charging on board;
vent gas - flammable and toxic, able to accumulate in an enclosed vehicle space and produce a gas explosion rather than a simple fire;
re-ignition hours or days after apparent extinction, defeating a normal fire-out judgement;

mis-declaration and concealment - cells as cargo may be undeclared or wrongly classified, and a battery electric vehicle is not a labelled package at all, so the energy is invisible to the stowage plan.

blocks.h: 3. Step 2 - assessing the risk on a ro-ro deck

blocks.p: Risk is frequency times consequence, estimated from casualty returns, incident and near-miss data, cell testing and fire modelling - with the Rev.2 requirement that the reliability, uncertainty and validity of that data be assessed and reported rather than assumed.

ul: Frequency is low per vehicle but rising with fleet electrification, and exposure is concentrated - one deck may hold thousands of units;

consequence escalates because a ro-ro space is a large undivided volume, vehicles stowed centimetres apart, with no cargo-hold fire divisions and ramps and ventilation trunks carrying heat and smoke between decks;
on a ro-pax the dominant risk is to life; on a pure car and truck carrier it is total loss of the ship, and a series of well-known casualties supplied the evidence;
manual firefighting on a loaded deck is near impossible, so the model must assume fixed systems and boundaries are what will actually be available.

blocks.h: 4. Steps 3 and 4 - risk control options and whether they pay

blocks.p: Risk control options are generated and grouped, then tested by cost-benefit assessment using indices such as the cost of averting a fatality, so a measure is recommended only where the safety gain justifies the cost across the world fleet:

ul: detection - earlier, better-located, individually identifiable so the seat of fire is known, with combined smoke and heat sensing;
suppression - drencher and water-based systems of adequate coverage and capacity, aligned with detection sections so the right section operates;
containment - insulated boundaries, ventilation shut-down and control of openings;
operational and design - state-of-charge limits on shipment, segregation and dedicated stowage, restrictions on charging at sea, video monitoring, crew procedures;
options are ranked, and those effective but disproportionately costly are rejected transparently - which is why the outcome is a specific set of measures rather than everything technically possible.

blocks.h: 5. Step 5 - what the recommendations actually became

blocks.p: The risk-based work on ro-ro fire safety - notably the EMSA FIRESAFE I and FIRESAFE II studies of fire dynamics, system performance and operational factors - entered the regulatory system in two stages:

ul: MSC.1/Circ.1615, Interim Guidelines for Minimizing the Incidence and Consequences of Fires in Ro-Ro Spaces and Special Category Spaces, carried key outcomes into guidance while mandatory work continued;

resolution MSC.550(108) then amended SOLAS chapter II-2 regulations 7 and 20 and MSC.555(108) amended FSS Code chapters 7 and 9, both adopted at MSC 108 in May 2024 and in force on 1 January 2026 - five weeks before this examination;

requirements include individually identifiable fixed detection with combined smoke and heat detectors, detection aligned with deluge sections, detection on weather decks used for vehicles, an effective video monitoring system with at least seven days of replay at a continuously manned control station, and A-60 boundaries on passenger ships carrying more than 36 passengers;
they apply to ships constructed on or after 1 January 2026, existing ships in scope complying not later than the first survey on or after 1 January 2028;
further amendments aimed at new energy vehicles were still in development, so the regulatory answer is partly delivered and continuing.

blocks.h: 6. b) Measures by stakeholder

ul: IMO - complete the new-energy-vehicle amendments, keep IMDG provisions current, maintain interim guidance meanwhile;
flag State and class - approve and survey the amended detection, suppression and boundary arrangements, and issue guidance ahead of the compliance dates;
shipper, manufacturer and packer - correct IMDG classification, packing and marking, state-of-charge control, testing and quality control, and no offering of damaged, defective or recalled batteries;
port and terminal - screen and refuse visibly damaged vehicles, check declared state of charge, separate electric vehicles in marshalling areas, inform the ship promptly;
ship operator - a written stowage and segregation policy, limits on charging on board, training in lithium fire behaviour, vehicle-deck drills, thermal imaging, and a plan that assumes re-ignition;

ship's staff - verify cargo against the declaration, maintain detection and drencher readiness, patrol during and after loading, and fight fire by early activation of fixed systems and boundary cooling rather than entering a loaded deck;
insurers and industry bodies - loss-prevention guidance, incident and near-miss data sharing, and premium signals rewarding compliant stowage - the same data that feeds the next FSA.

blocks.h: Why this structure scores

blocks.p: The 10-mark limb is a method question, and method questions are marked on whether the method is visible. Naming the five steps and then walking the cargo through them is what separates a top answer from a general essay about battery fires. Step 5 is where most candidates stop short: an FSA that produces no recommendation has not been applied, so ending with the actual resolutions is what closes the loop.

blocks.h: Why FSA exists at all

blocks.p: Before FSA, IMO regulation was largely reactive - a casualty happened, and a rule followed. FSA was introduced after the Herald of Free Enterprise and Piper Alpha era to allow the Organization to act proactively and proportionately, on evidence rather than on the emotional weight of the most recent disaster, and to be able to say publicly why a proposed rule was or was not worth its cost. That is why the Guidelines insist on auditability, traceability and the explicit reporting of uncertainty: an FSA is as much an accountability document as a technical one.

blocks.h: The lithium hazard in engineering terms

blocks.p: Thermal runaway begins when a cell's internal temperature passes the point at which exothermic decomposition of the electrolyte and cathode outpaces heat loss. The decomposition liberates oxygen from the cathode material, which is why the reaction sustains itself without air and why smothering agents - CO2, foam blanket, an inert atmosphere - do not stop it. Cooling is the only lever the ship holds, and it works by removing heat from cells that have not yet reached onset temperature, so its real objective is to stop propagation to neighbouring vehicles rather than to extinguish the cell already in runaway. That is also why re-ignition is normal rather than surprising: the cells that were merely heated may still cross the threshold hours later.

blocks.h: Vehicles, containers and packages are three different regulatory problems

ul: Cells and batteries as cargo - dangerous goods under the IMDG Code, class 9, with UN numbers such as 3480 and 3481 for lithium-ion and 3090 and 3091 for lithium-metal, subject to packing, marking, documentation and segregation.
Batteries in or with equipment - the same UN family but different provisions, and often carried under exceptions.

A battery electric vehicle - carried as a vehicle, not as a declared dangerous goods package. This is the regulatory gap: the ship may know exactly how many tonnes of declared lithium cells she has in containers, and not know how much energy is sitting on the vehicle deck.

blocks.h: Common mistakes

ul: Describing FSA as a shipboard risk assessment. Read the circular's title.
Listing the five steps and then never using them - a hazard essay wearing an FSA hat.
Saying water must never be used on a lithium fire. Cooling and boundary protection with copious water is the accepted tactic.
Saying the fire can be smothered with CO2. The reaction supplies its own oxidant.
Declaring the fire out when flames stop. Re-ignition must be assumed and monitored for.
Treating a battery electric vehicle as though it were declared dangerous goods, or vice versa.

blocks.h: Examiner traps

ul: 'In vehicles and containers and in RORO ships' - three carriage modes are named deliberately, and an answer that only discusses containers has ignored a third of the question.
'Application of formal safety assessment' - the mark is in the application, not the definition.
Limb (b) says stakeholders, plural. An answer confined to what the ship's staff should do cannot score well; the chain begins at the cell manufacturer.

blocks.h: Likely oral follow-up

ul: A car on your vehicle deck is smoking. What are your first four actions?
Why will CO2 not put out a lithium-ion fire?
How would you know a battery electric vehicle had been loaded?
What does 'individually identifiable' mean in a detection system, and why does it matter here?
When can you say this fire is out?

blocks.h: Memory framework

blocks.p: The method as a funnel: what could go wrong, how bad and how often, what could we do, is it worth it, what do we recommend. The hazard in four words that each defeat a normal tactic: self-oxidising, propagating, venting, re-igniting. The remedy chain for limb (b) runs down the supply chain: regulator, class, shipper, terminal, operator, ship.

blocks.h: Uncertainty and currency

blocks.p: Two limitations are stated rather than concealed. First, no dedicated published IMO Formal Safety Assessment study on lithium batteries in ro-ro carriage was located. The answer therefore explains how the FSA method applies to this cargo and identifies the FIRESAFE programme and the resulting amendments as the risk-based work that was actually done; it does not assert that a formal FSA submission on lithium batteries exists. Second, MIW holds no licensed SOLAS or FSS Code, so the amendment content rests on an authoritative class-society restatement. The dates matter unusually here: MSC.550(108) and MSC.555(108) had been in force for roughly five weeks at the date of this sitting, and the further new energy vehicle amendments were still in development - so an answer written today must not project the later position back onto February 2026.

quick_revision.recall_15s: (a) FSA is MSC-MEPC.2/Circ.12/Rev.2, 9 April 2018 - Revised Guidelines for Formal Safety Assessment for use in the IMO rule-making process. It is how the Organization decides what a rule should say; it is not a shipboard risk assessment. Five steps: 1 hazard identification, 2 risk analysis, 3 risk control options, 4 cost-benefit assessment, 5 recommendations for decision-making, with uncertainty required to be reported. Applied to lithium batteries: hazards are thermal runaway that is self-sustaining and needs no external oxygen, damaged or mis-declared cells, high state of charge, flammable and toxic vent gas with explosion potential, re-ignition, and concealment inside a vehicle. Risk escalates on a ro-ro deck because vehicles are close-stowed in a large undivided space with ramps and ventilation paths. Control options are detection, suppression, containment and operational limits, tested by cost-benefit. retrieval_cards.prompt: What is FSA actually for, and what is it not?
retrieval_cards.answer: It is a structured, auditable methodology for the IMO's rule-making process - deciding whether and what to regulate. It is not a shipboard risk assessment, a permit-to-work system or a job hazard analysis.
retrieval_cards.why: The circular's own title says 'for use in the IMO rule-making process'. Missing this turns the whole answer into a generic safety essay.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Why is thermal runaway in a lithium-ion cell so difficult to fight on a vehicle deck?
retrieval_cards.answer: It is self-sustaining and does not require external oxygen, so smothering does not stop it; it propagates cell to cell; it vents flammable and toxic gas that can accumulate and explode; and it can re-ignite hours or days after apparent extinction.
retrieval_cards.why: Each of these four properties defeats one of the ship's normal fire tactics, which is why the hazard needed new rules.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Which instruments changed the fire safety requirements for vehicle and ro-ro spaces, and when did they take effect?
retrieval_cards.answer: MSC.550(108) amending SOLAS chapter II-2 regulations 7 and 20, and MSC.555(108) amending FSS Code chapters 7 and 9. Both were adopted in May 2024 and entered into force on 1 January 2026, applying to ships constructed on or after that date, with existing ships in scope by the first survey on or after 1 January 2028.
retrieval_cards.why: They had been in force for about five weeks at the date of this sitting, which is exactly the kind of currency the examiner rewards.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Should water be used on a lithium-ion vehicle fire on a ro-ro deck?
retrieval_cards.answer: Yes - copious water for cooling and boundary protection is the accepted tactic. The aim is to remove heat and stop propagation to adjacent vehicles, not to extinguish the cell reaction, which cannot be smothered because it generates its own oxidant.
retrieval_cards.why: The widespread belief that water must be avoided is wrong and dangerous, and it is a favourite oral follow-up.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Why is a battery electric vehicle harder to regulate as cargo than a container of cells?
retrieval_cards.answer: Cells shipped as cargo are declared and classified under the IMDG Code, with packing, marking and segregation requirements. A vehicle driven aboard is carried as a vehicle, so the energy travels concealed inside it with no package, no declaration and no segregation, which is the gap the new-energy-vehicle work is trying to close.

questions.understand_first: Two things must be kept apart, because the question mixes them. Formal Safety Assessment is not a risk assessment you carry out on board - it is the structured method the regulator uses to decide whether a rule is worth making, and whether it would be worth what it costs. So this answer is written from the rule-maker's chair, not the Chief Engineer's. The cargo is what makes it interesting. A lithium battery fire is not an ordinary vehicle fire: it generates its own oxygen, so smothering does not stop it; it can reignite hours after it appears to be out; and it sits on a ro-ro deck, which is close to the worst possible geometry - a long undivided space, vehicles packed tight, and a fixed system designed for a fuel fire. Work the standard steps against those facts and the control options almost choose themselves: detect earlier, contain locally, cool for far longer. And be honest that some options cost more than the harm they prevent, which is precisely what the cost-benefit step is for.

blocks.h: 1. (A) What the human element means in STCW

blocks.p: STCW refuses to treat competence as something time served automatically confers. It replaces experience with demonstrated competence, then addresses the conditions - fitness, rest, teamwork and company responsibility - under which competence can actually be exercised. The instrument is the STCW Convention and Code, 1978, as amended, most significantly by the Manila amendments of 2010, in force from 1 January 2012.

blocks.h: 2. Competence-based standards

ul: The Part A tables of competence specify, for every function and level, the competence required, the knowledge, understanding and proficiency behind it, the methods for demonstrating it and the criteria for evaluating it - so assessment is against a published standard, not an examiner's impression.
Part A is mandatory; Part B is guidance - a distinction worth stating.

The Manila amendments added mandatory training in leadership and teamworking at operational level and leadership and managerial skill at management level - where engine-room and bridge resource management, situational awareness and workload management enter the Convention. It is the explicit recognition that technically competent individuals still fail as a team.
Regulation I/6 governs training and assessment, and regulation I/8 requires a quality standards system, so the training system itself is audited rather than assumed.
Regulation I/11 requires periodic revalidation, and chapter VI mandatory safety familiarisation and basic training before a seafarer is assigned duties.

blocks.h: 3. Fitness for duty - the physical human being

ul: Regulation VIII/1 requires each Administration, for the purpose of preventing fatigue, to establish and enforce rest periods for watchkeeping personnel and for those with designated safety, security and pollution-prevention duties in accordance with section A-VIII/1, and to require that watch systems are arranged so that efficiency is not impaired by fatigue.

The Manila-amended A-VIII/1 minimum rest is 10 hours in any 24-hour period and 77 hours in any 7-day period. The daily rest may be divided into no more than two periods, one of which shall be at least 6 hours, and the interval between consecutive periods of rest shall not exceed 14 hours.

Authorised exceptions are tightly conditioned: weekly rest may not fall below 70 hours in any 7-day period, exceptions from the 77-hour norm may not run for more than two consecutive weeks, and daily rest may then be divided into no more than three periods.
The Manila amendments also introduced alcohol limits for masters, officers and other seafarers with designated safety, security and environmental duties.
Regulation I/9 sets medical fitness standards, and regulation VIII/2 with section A-VIII/2 governs watchkeeping arrangements and principles.

blocks.h: 4. Responsibility placed on companies and Administrations

blocks.p: Regulation I/14 makes the company responsible for ensuring seafarers hold valid certificates, are familiarised with their duties and the ship's arrangements, and that documentation is maintained - so the human element is not left as an individual's problem. Administrations operate quality standards and are subject to independent evaluation and reporting to IMO.

blocks.h: 5. The 2024 amendments - the human element widened

ul: Resolution MSC.560(108), the 2024 amendments to Part A of the STCW Code, was adopted on 23 May 2024 and entered into force on 1 January 2026. It is therefore in force at this sitting and belongs in any answer on how the Code addresses the human element.

It adds to table A-VI/1-4 in section A-VI/1 of chapter VI a competence on contributing to the prevention of and response to violence and harassment, including sexual harassment, bullying and sexual assault.

Why it matters for this question: everything above treats the human element as competence, fitness for duty and teamworking. This amendment is the first time the Code addresses the seafarer's safety from other people on board - a different axis of the human element, and the one an examiner is most likely to reward as current knowledge.
Transitional effect: certificates already held remain valid until they expire, with the additional training delivered by approved institutions and recorded on completion.

blocks.h: 6. (B) The IMO guidance on fatigue

blocks.p: The current guidance is MSC.1/Circ.1598, "Guidelines on fatigue", of 24 January 2019, approved at the 100th session of the Maritime Safety Committee and finalized by the HTW Sub-Committee. It supersedes MSC/Circ.1014 of 2001. It is recommendatory, not mandatory - the binding rest-hour requirements remain in STCW chapter VIII and in MLC 2006. The Guidelines are arranged in six modules, each addressed to a different party:

ul: Module 1 - Fatigue: what it is, and its causes, grouped as sleep and rest, the biological clock and circadian rhythm, health and stress, environmental factors such as noise, vibration and motion, sleep disorders and operational factors. It defines sleep debt as insufficient accumulated sleep over multiple consecutive 24-hour periods.
Module 2 - Fatigue and the Company: assessing, mitigating and managing fatigue risk in the safety management system, in manning decisions and in scheduling.

Module 3 - Fatigue and the Seafarer: practical guidance for the master, officers and ratings on sleep quality, diet, and the limits of countermeasures - notably that caffeine is not a substitute for sleep.
Module 4 - Fatigue Awareness and Training.
Module 5 - Fatigue and Ship Design: mitigation designed in - accommodation location, noise, vibration, lighting and habitability.
Module 6 - Fatigue, the Administration and Port State Authorities: how regulators and inspectors should approach it.

blocks.h: 7. How the guidance and the rules fit together

blocks.p: The Guidelines are explicit that hours of rest are set by a prescriptive formula in STCW chapter VIII, and that complying with the formula is not the same as being rested: managers must allow for circadian rhythm and sleep debt, and - in the Guidelines' words - rest means rest, not substituting a different form of work. The same theme runs through MLC 2006 Regulations 2.3, 2.4 and 2.7. A management-level engineer should therefore treat recorded compliance as the floor, and a rest-hour record that is always exactly compliant as a warning rather than a reassurance.

blocks.h: Why this structure scores

blocks.p: Two printed limbs of 8 marks each, so split the answer evenly and head each limb clearly. Limb A rewards structure - competence tables, fitness for duty, company responsibility - and limb B rewards naming the actual circular. A candidate who writes generally about tiredness for the second limb without producing MSC.1/Circ.1598 and its module structure will lose most of eight marks, because "the IMO guidance" is a specific document.

blocks.h: The organising idea for limb A

blocks.p: STCW attacks the human element on three fronts, and saying so gives the limb a spine: can they do it (competence standards, assessed against published criteria), are they fit to do it now (fitness for duty - rest, medical, alcohol), and who is responsible for making that possible (regulation I/14, the company). The Manila amendments strengthened all three, and added the fourth dimension the older Convention lacked - can they work as a team, through mandatory leadership and teamworking training.

blocks.h: The numbers you must get right

blocks.p: 10 hours in any 24, and 77 hours in any 7 days. Divided into no more than two periods, one of at least 6 hours, with no more than 14 hours between consecutive rest periods. Exceptions may not go below 70 hours in any 7 days and may not run more than two consecutive weeks. Learn 10, 77, 2, 6, 14, 70 - and be careful, because 70 and 77 are both real figures doing different jobs: 77 is the norm, 70 is the floor under an authorised exception. Quoting 70 as the normal requirement is the classic error, and it is exactly the trap that a pre-2010 copy of the Code will lead you into.

blocks.h: Currency - what applies and what does not

blocks.p: The operative regime is STCW 1978 as amended, with the Manila amendments in force from 1 January 2012. A comprehensive review of the STCW Convention and Code has been under way through the HTW Sub-Committee with completion targeted around 2027 - one of the acknowledged gaps being the treatment of hours of rest. Nothing had been adopted at the date of this paper. So write the Manila regime as current, and mention the review only as work in progress. Do not present any reviewed text as though it were in force.

blocks.h: Common mistakes

ul: Answering limb B without naming MSC.1/Circ.1598 and the circular it replaced, MSC/Circ.1014.
Treating the fatigue Guidelines as mandatory. They are recommendatory; the binding requirements are STCW chapter VIII and MLC 2006.
Quoting 70 hours as the normal weekly rest. 77 is the norm; 70 is the minimum where an exception has been authorised.
Confusing hours of rest with hours of work. MLC permits either a maximum-hours-of-work or a minimum-hours-of-rest approach; STCW A-VIII/1 is expressed as minimum rest.

Writing about STCW competence generally without mentioning that the Manila amendments made leadership and teamworking training mandatory - that is the human-element addition the question is really pointing at.
Forgetting regulation I/14. The human element is not only about the seafarer; the company carries defined obligations.

blocks.h: Examiner traps

blocks.p:
"Your rest-hour records show full compliance. Is your crew rested?" Not necessarily, and the Guidelines say so - the formula is prescriptive, and quality of rest depends on circadian rhythm and accumulated sleep debt. Records that are always exactly compliant deserve suspicion, not comfort.

"Is coffee a fatigue countermeasure?" The Guidelines address it directly: caffeine can improve alertness temporarily but is not a substitute for adequate sleep and rest, and can interfere with sleep afterwards.

"Where do the fatigue Guidelines actually bite on board?" Through the safety management system - Module 2 is addressed to the company, so fatigue risk belongs in manning, scheduling and the ISM Code procedures rather than being left to individual willpower.

blocks.h: Likely oral follow-up

ul: Which circular contains the IMO fatigue Guidelines? MSC.1/Circ.1598 of 24 January 2019, approved at MSC 100, replacing MSC/Circ.1014.
How many modules, and who are they addressed to? Six - fatigue itself, the company, the seafarer, awareness and training, ship design, and the Administration and port State authorities.
State the minimum hours of rest. 10 hours in any 24-hour period and 77 in any 7-day period; no more than two periods, one at least 6 hours; intervals not exceeding 14 hours.
When do the Manila amendments date from? Adopted 2010, in force 1 January 2012.
Which STCW regulation makes the company responsible? Regulation I/14 - valid certificates, familiarisation and documentation.
Are the fatigue Guidelines mandatory? No. STCW chapter VIII and MLC 2006 carry the mandatory requirements; the Guidelines are recommendatory.

blocks.h: Memory framework

blocks.p: Limb A in four questions: CAN THEY - ARE THEY FIT - CAN THEY TEAM - WHO IS RESPONSIBLE. Competence tables; fitness for duty; leadership and teamworking; regulation I/14. Limb B by audience: WHAT IT IS - COMPANY - SEAFARER - TRAINING - SHIP - REGULATOR, which is the six modules in order. The numbers: 10 / 77 / 2 / 6 / 14, floor 70.

blocks.h: Uncertainty and source status

blocks.p: The fatigue limb is primary-verified: the circular number, date, approving session, the superseded circular and the six module titles were all read in the text of MSC.1/Circ.1598, as were the sleep-debt definition and the statement about the prescriptive STCW formula. The rest-hour figures carry a caveat worth recording. MIW holds no licensed copy of the STCW Convention and Code. An IMO circular copy of section A-VIII/1 was consulted first and turned out to be the pre-Manila 1995 text - five paragraphs, 70 hours per seven-day period, and no 14-hour interval rule. Taking it at face value would have produced a confidently wrong answer. The Manila-amended figures used here therefore come from a competent-authority notice reproducing the amended regime, which also confirms the 1 January 2012 entry into force. They are consistent across sources and are safe to use, but they sit at authoritative-secondary status rather than primary, and acquiring a licensed STCW Code would promote them. The lesson generalises: for an amended instrument, confirm which edition a source is reproducing before quoting a number from it.

questions.understand_first: The human element is not a soft topic bolted onto a technical convention. STCW treats it as three separate engineering problems: whether a person has a demonstrated capability, whether they are in a fit state to use it right now, and whose job it is to make that possible. blocks.h: 1. What the Act means by an unseaworthy ship

blocks.p: The Merchant Shipping Act 1958 does not define unseaworthiness in a definitions section. The description sits inside section 334, which provides that a ship is unseaworthy when the following are not such as to render her in every respect fit for the proposed voyage or service:

ul: the materials of which she is made and her construction;
the qualifications of the master;
the number, description and qualifications of the crew, including officers;
the weight, description and stowage of the cargo and ballast;
the condition of her hull and equipment, boilers and machinery.

blocks.p: Two features deserve emphasis. The test is relative - fitness for the proposed voyage or service - so a ship adequate for a sheltered coastal run may be unseaworthy for an ocean passage. And it is far wider than material condition: an undermanned ship, one whose officers hold the wrong certificates, or a well-maintained ship with badly stowed cargo is unseaworthy under the Act though nothing is mechanically defective.

blocks.h: 2. The offence, and the defences the Act allows

ul: s.334(1) - every person who sends or attempts to send an Indian ship to sea from any port in India in such an unseaworthy state that the life of any person is likely to be thereby endangered is guilty of an offence, unless he proves he used all reasonable means to insure her being sent to sea in a seaworthy state, or that going to sea in that state was reasonable and justifiable.
s.334(2) - a master who knowingly takes such a ship to sea commits the offence, with only the second defence.
s.334(3) permits a person charged to give evidence; s.334(4) provides that no prosecution shall be instituted except by, or with the consent of, the Central Government.

blocks.p: Liability is therefore not automatic: the threshold is danger to life, the defence burden lies on the accused, and the standard is reasonable means, not a guarantee.

blocks.h: 3. What an unsafe ship is, and the power to detain her

blocks.p: Section 336 addresses a different problem - stopping the ship rather than punishing anyone. An unsafe ship is one which, by reason of the defective condition of her hull, equipment or machinery, or by reason of overloading or improper loading, is unfit to proceed to sea without serious danger to human life, having regard to the nature of the service for which she is intended. The procedure is staged:

ol: the Central Government, having reason to believe on complaint or otherwise that she is unsafe, may order her provisionally detained for survey;
a written statement of the grounds must be served forthwith on the master;
the matter is referred to the court of survey for the port, or a competent person is appointed to survey and report;
on the report she is either released or finally detained.

blocks.h: 4. The real difference between the two

ul: Unseaworthy is a state; unsafe is a trigger for a power. Section 334 describes a condition and attaches criminal liability to sending her to sea in it; section 336 describes a condition entitling the Government to stop her.
One looks backwards, the other forwards. The offence punishes a decision taken; detention prevents the voyage happening at all.
Unseaworthiness is the wider concept - it expressly takes in crew numbers and qualifications and the stowage of cargo and ballast. The unsafe-ship definition lists a narrower set of causes.
The thresholds differ - life likely to be endangered under s.334; unfitness to proceed without serious danger to human life under s.336.
Practically, a ship unsafe within s.336 will invariably be unseaworthy within s.334, but a ship may be unseaworthy - one deck officer short - without being unsafe.

blocks.h: 5. The owner's obligation to the crew

blocks.p: Section 335 converts seaworthiness from a matter between owner and cargo into a duty owed to the people on board. In every contract of service, express or implied, between the owner of an Indian ship and the master or any seaman, and in every contract of apprenticeship, there is implied - notwithstanding any agreement to the contrary - an obligation that the owner, the master and every agent charged with loading, preparing her for sea or sending her to sea shall use all reasonable means to ensure the seaworthiness of the ship for the voyage at the time when the voyage commences, and shall keep her in a seaworthy state during the voyage.

Three points follow. It is non-excludable - a crew-agreement term waiving it is void. It is a due diligence standard, not a guarantee of result. And it is continuing through the voyage, unlike the doctrine of stages. It also binds persons other than the owner - the loading agent is named.

blocks.h: 6. How the obligation is policed, and what changed afterwards

blocks.p: Section 335(2) allows the Central Government to arrange a survey of the hull, equipment or machinery. In practice the duty is policed through the wider system - class and flag State statutory survey and certification, ISM auditing and port State control under SOLAS I/19 - with s.336 detention as the last resort.

One point of currency must be stated rather than assumed. The Merchant Shipping Act 1958 was the operative law at the date of this examination. It was repealed by section 324(1) of the Merchant Shipping Act 2025, in force 15 March 2026 - some five weeks after this paper was sat. The answer is therefore correctly given on the 1958 Act.

blocks.h: Why this structure scores

blocks.p: The stem asks three questions and prints no limbs, so the examiner has no printed structure to mark against and will mark against the three questions asked. Answering them in the order asked, with the middle one made explicitly comparative, is what makes the script easy to mark. The comparison in step 4 is the highest-value paragraph in the answer and the one most often missing: candidates define both terms and then never say how they differ, which is literally what was asked.

blocks.h: Why the Act splits the idea in two

blocks.p: A criminal offence needs fault, a trial and proof beyond reasonable doubt, and it operates after the event - which is no use at all to the crew of a ship that is about to sail. An administrative detention power needs only a reasonable belief and can act in hours. The 1958 Act therefore does both: section 334 attaches consequences to a decision, and section 336 provides the fast preventive lever, with a survey and a right to be told the grounds as the safeguards against its misuse. Recognising that the two sections exist to solve different problems is the whole of the distinction.

blocks.h: Seaworthiness has three different legal lives - keep them apart

ul: Statutory and criminal - MSA 1958 s.334, this question. A state of the ship, punishable, with a due-diligence defence.
Contractual, owed to the crew - MSA 1958 s.335. Implied, non-excludable, continuing through the voyage.

Insurance and carriage - a warranty or a duty of due diligence, depending on whether the policy is a voyage or time policy and on the contract of carriage. Under Indian law that is the Marine Insurance Act 1963, not the English Act of 1906, and a breach affects recovery rather than attracting a penalty.

blocks.p: The examiner asks about the first two. Answering about the third is the commonest way to lose this question.

blocks.h: Common mistakes

ul: Describing seaworthiness in general engineering terms without quoting the section 334 formula.
Leaving crew numbers, certification and stowage out of the definition - they are expressly inside it.
Treating unseaworthy and unsafe as interchangeable, or asserting the difference is one of degree only.
Saying the owner guarantees seaworthiness. The duty is to use all reasonable means.
Forgetting that the section 335 duty continues during the voyage.
Answering under the English Marine Insurance Act 1906 or the doctrine of stages.
Answering under the Merchant Shipping Act 2025, which was not in force on the examination date.

blocks.h: Examiner traps

ul: 'Within the meaning of the Merchant Shipping Act (MSA), 1958, as amended' - the examiner is asking for the statutory meaning, and a general definition cannot score the top band.
'What according to you is the difference' invites an opinion, but the marks are for the legal difference, not a preference.
'Obligations of owners to crew' - plural owners, and section 335 also binds the master and the loading agent, so an answer confined to the registered owner is incomplete.

blocks.h: Memory framework

blocks.p: The three sections are consecutive and in logical order: 334 the state, 335 the duty, 336 the power. Inside 334, the definition runs bow to stern and then outward to the people: materials, construction, master, crew, cargo and ballast, hull, equipment, boilers and machinery - fit in every respect for the proposed voyage. The two phrases worth memorising word for word are 'fit in every respect for the proposed voyage or service' and 'notwithstanding any agreement to the contrary'.

questions.understand_first: These are two different legal tools, not two words for the same idea. Unseaworthy describes a state of the ship and is the trigger for a criminal offence and for a duty owed to the crew - it looks at fault and at responsibility. blocks.h: 1. a) What a general average act is

blocks.p: General average is the principle that where one interest is deliberately sacrificed to save the whole, the loss is shared rateably by all the interests saved. It is given effect not by statute but by the York-Antwerp Rules, incorporated by contract; the current edition is the 2016 Rules. In India the statutory definition appears in section 66 of the Marine Insurance Act 1963.

Rule A states the test: there is a general average act when, and only when, any extraordinary sacrifice or expenditure is intentionally and reasonably made or incurred for the common safety for the purpose of preserving from peril the property involved in a common maritime adventure. The words when, and only when matter - the conditions are cumulative.

blocks.h: 2. The essential features, all of which must be present

ol: Extraordinary - outside the ordinary incidents of the voyage. Fuel burnt on a normal passage, or wear and tear, is not; nor is anything the owner was already bound to do.

Intentional - a deliberate act. This is the heart of the doctrine: accidental loss, however catastrophic, is never general average. Cargo washed overboard is particular average; cargo jettisoned is general average.

Reasonable - judged on the circumstances as they appeared at the time, reinforced by the Rule Paramount: in no case shall there be any allowance for sacrifice or expenditure unless reasonably made or incurred.
For the common safety - for the whole adventure. Action to save only the ship, or only the cargo, is not general average.
A real peril - real and substantial, though it need not be immediate or inevitable.

A common maritime adventure, and a useful result - more than one interest at risk, or there is nobody to contribute, and something must be saved, since contribution is assessed on the values preserved.

blocks.h: 3. What is excluded, and who must prove it

ul: Rule C allows only the direct consequence of the general average act, and excludes demurrage, loss of market, any loss or expense by reason of delay and any indirect loss whatsoever, and environmental damage or loss consequent on the escape of pollutants.

Rule D - rights to contribution are not affected though the event was due to the fault of a party, without prejudice to remedies or defences for that fault. Contribution and liability are separate questions.
Rule E - the onus of proof is on the party claiming; failing particulars within twelve months the adjuster may estimate.

blocks.h: 4. b) Testing the casualty against the rules

blocks.p: Taking the Rule A elements against the facts - aground, the main engine worked ahead and astern to shake her loose, bearings burnt through excessive load:

ul: extraordinary - burnt bearings from deliberate overload are outside the ordinary incidents of the voyage, and are not wear and tear;
intentional - working the engine hard astern to refloat is a deliberate act of the master;
for the common safety - a grounded vessel endangers ship, cargo and freight alike;
direct consequence - the damage arose immediately from that act, satisfying Rule C;
peril - the one element the question does not settle, and it must be examined rather than assumed.

blocks.h: 5. Rule VII, which decides the point

blocks.p: The Rules deal with this precise situation expressly. Rule VII, Damage to Machinery and Boilers: Damage caused to any machinery and boilers of a ship which is ashore and in a position of peril, in endeavouring to refloat, shall be allowed in general average when shown to have arisen from an actual intention to float the ship for the common safety at the risk of such damage; but where a ship is afloat no loss or damage caused by working the propelling machinery and boilers shall in any circumstances be allowed as general average.

Three conditions and one absolute bar. The conditions: ashore; in a position of peril; machinery worked with an actual intention to float her for the common safety, at the risk of such damage. The bar: if she is afloat, machinery damage from working the engines is never allowed.

blocks.h: 6. Conclusion, and what must be done to sustain it

blocks.p: Yes - the bearing damage can be included in general average, provided the Rule VII conditions are established. The first is satisfied: she was aground. The other two are questions of evidence:

ul: Position of peril. Hard aground on a falling tide, on a lee shore or on rock, taking water, or with weather deteriorating - peril is readily shown. Merely touching soft ground in sheltered water, certain to float on the next tide, is not; the act was one of convenience and the claim fails.

Actual intention, accepting the risk. The master must have worked the engine knowing it might be damaged and accepted that to free the ship. Engines worked to test the ground, or in routine hope of coming off, do not meet the rule.

Evidence. Timed deck and engine log entries, the master's recorded assessment of the danger, engine parameters and alarms, soundings, weather, owner or salvor advice. The onus is on the claimant under Rule E.

blocks.p: Two points complete the answer. The damage must be reasonable in extent under the Rule Paramount. And by Rule D, negligent navigation causing the grounding does not lose the right to contribution, though cargo may resist under the contract of carriage. In practice the owner declares general average, appoints an average adjuster and releases cargo against a general average bond and an average guarantee.

blocks.h: Why this structure scores

blocks.p: Limb (b) is worth 8 marks and asks for justification, which means the marks are in the reasoning chain, not the verdict. An answer that says 'yes, it is general average because the engine was used to save the ship' has given the conclusion and none of the justification. Running the Rule A elements first and then reaching Rule VII lets the candidate show the general test and the specific rule, and - crucially - identify the two facts the question deliberately leaves open.

blocks.h: The question is testing whether you know Rule VII exists

blocks.p: This scenario is not a general knowledge problem; it is drafted straight onto a named rule. Every element in the stem maps to a phrase in Rule VII: ran aground to 'ashore', main engine used ahead and astern to shake the vessel loose to 'in endeavouring to refloat', bearings got burnt to 'damage caused to any machinery'. A candidate who cites Rule A alone can reach the right answer by general reasoning and will score respectably; one who cites Rule VII and quotes the afloat proviso is demonstrably answering the question that was set.

blocks.h: Why the law inverts ordinary intuition

blocks.p: The rule that deliberate damage is recoverable and accidental damage is not looks perverse until you see what it is for. General average is a cost-allocation mechanism, not a compensation scheme. Its purpose is to remove the master's conflict of interest at the moment of crisis: if the shipowner alone bore the cost of sacrificing the ship's machinery, or of jettisoning cargo, the person best placed to save the adventure would have a financial reason to hesitate. By promising that a reasonable, deliberate sacrifice will be shared by everyone who benefits, the doctrine makes the right decision the cheap decision. Accidental loss needs no such encouragement, which is why it stays where it falls.

blocks.h: The afloat proviso, and why it is absolute

blocks.p: Rule VII's second half is unusually emphatic - in any circumstances. The reason is evidential rather than moral. When a ship is afloat, working the propelling machinery is exactly what she is supposed to do, so there is no way to distinguish an extraordinary sacrifice from ordinary use, and a claim would be unanswerable and unverifiable. When she is ashore, the act is visibly abnormal and the intention can be tested. The Rules solve the evidential problem by drawing a bright line.

blocks.h: Common mistakes

ul: Concluding 'no' because the damage was caused by overload. Overload was the mechanism; the question is whether it was accepted deliberately, in peril, to refloat.
Concluding 'yes' unconditionally, without identifying peril and intention as things to be proved.
Citing only Rule A when Rule VII is directly on point.
Forgetting the afloat proviso, which is half of Rule VII and the source of the best follow-up question.
Saying negligence defeats general average. Rule D says it does not - it may found a separate claim.
Confusing general average with salvage or with particular average.
Calling the York-Antwerp Rules a convention or statute. They are contractual terms.

blocks.h: Examiner traps

ul: The stem says a large vessel ran aground and stops. It does not say she was in peril, and that omission is deliberate - it is the fact the answer must treat as conditional.
'Give proper justification' is a direction about form. A bare verdict cannot score, however correct.

Limb (a) is a quotation - 'General average is based on certain essential features' - and quotation stems reward candidates who enumerate the features explicitly rather than writing an essay around them.

ul: Same damage, but the vessel is afloat and working engines against a gale to hold off a lee shore. General average?

blocks.h: Memory framework

blocks.p: Learn Rule A as a sentence - every essential feature is one of its words, so the definition and the list are the same thing. For the applied limb, hold Rule VII as four conditions and one bar: ashore, in peril, intending to float, accepting the risk - never if afloat. And hold the one-line principle that answers most general average scenarios: somebody must have chosen it, on purpose, for everybody.

blocks.h: Uncertainty and jurisdiction

blocks.p: The York-Antwerp Rules are contractual, not statutory: they apply because the bill of lading or charterparty incorporates them, and which edition applies is therefore a question about the contract. The 2016 edition was read and is cited here. Rule VII is materially unchanged across the 1994, 2004 and 2016 editions, so the conclusion in limb (b) does not depend on the choice - but the answer states the dependency rather than assuming it. Section 66 of the Indian Marine Insurance Act 1963 is cited as a pointer to the Indian statutory position; it was not read in the statute for this question and the answer does not rest on its wording. Note for candidates that the Indian Act is the 1963 Act, not the English Marine Insurance Act 1906.

questions.understand_first: General average is the one place in marine practice where deliberately damaging your own ship can be recovered, and accidental damage cannot. That inversion is the whole subject. If a bearing fails on passage through overload, it is the owner's loss alone; if the same bearing is burnt because the master knowingly drove the engine hard to save the ship and cargo from a common danger, every interest that was saved contributes to it. So when a scenario asks whether damage is general average, do not ask how bad it was - ask whether somebody chose it, on purpose, for everybody's benefit.
