blocks.h: 1. Adoption is not entry into force

blocks.p: A convention is adopted either by the competent IMO organ - Assembly, MSC, MEPC or Legal Committee - or by a diplomatic conference. Adoption settles the text and does no more: it binds no State, and an adopted convention may never enter into force at all. The text is then opened for signature and deposited with the Secretary-General of IMO as depositary.

blocks.h: 2. How a State expresses consent to be bound

blocks.p: Between adoption and entry into force sits the step that matters: each State must express its consent to be bound, by one of three routes -

ul: signature alone, where the treaty so provides or the negotiating States so agreed;
signature subject to ratification, acceptance or approval, the normal course for multilateral conventions;
accession, where the State did not sign within the signature period.

blocks.p: In the second and third cases the State is bound only on depositing a formal instrument with the depositary, who records it, counts it towards the entry into force condition and notifies all other States.

blocks.h: 3. The two terms the question names

blocks.p: (ii) Signature subject to ratification, acceptance or approval. The State signs, but signature does not bind it; it indicates an intention to proceed. The State becomes a party only on later depositing an instrument of ratification. Its modern purpose is to give the State time to enact domestic legislation and satisfy constitutional requirements before committing internationally. Acceptance and approval are the same act under less formal names, used where a constitution does not demand the fuller procedure: VCLT Article 14(2) provides that consent is expressed by acceptance or approval under conditions similar to those which apply to ratification. In legal effect the three are identical.

(i) Accession. The means by which a State becomes party to a treaty it did not sign - because the signature period closed, or it was not a negotiating State. It is a single step: no prior signature, simply deposit of an instrument of accession, permitted by VCLT Article 15 where the treaty so provides. Once deposited it has exactly the same legal effect as ratification. The difference is the route, not the destination.

blocks.h: 4. The entry into force provision, and why it matters

blocks.p: Every convention contains a final clause fixing entry into force, normally a threshold of acceptances plus a waiting period. Its importance is fourfold:

ul: it prevents an instrument binding a handful of States while the rest operate to another standard, which would distort competition;
it fixes a certain date from which obligations, surveys and certificates run, so Administrations, ROs, owners and yards work to one deadline;
it provides the interval for flag States to legislate, class to develop rules and industry to build or retrofit;
it gives legitimacy - a convention in force across most world tonnage is enforceable through port State control against the remainder, which is what makes no more favourable treatment work.

blocks.h: 5. Conventions of an important technical nature

blocks.p: For a convention of important technical nature - one dictating construction, equipment or operation - States observe a stiffer double condition: a number of States and a percentage of the gross tonnage of the world's merchant shipping. A count of States alone could be met by many small flags while the major fleets stayed outside, leaving the convention in force on paper and irrelevant at sea.

ul: SOLAS 1974 - adopted 1 November 1974, requiring not less than 25 States whose combined merchant fleets constitute not less than 50 per cent of the gross tonnage of the world's merchant shipping; in force 25 May 1980.
The 1978 MARPOL Protocol - in force twelve months after not less than fifteen States constituting not less than fifty per cent of world merchant shipping gross tonnage had become Parties.

blocks.p: Older conventions typically required two-thirds of contracting States, which occasionally meant more acceptances were needed to bring an instrument into force than to amend it.

blocks.h: 6. Keeping the convention current once in force

blocks.p: A technical convention is worthless if it cannot keep pace, and explicit acceptance failed on that point: amendments to the 1960 SOLAS Convention adopted between 1966 and 1973 never received enough acceptances and none entered into force.

IMO's answer was the tacit acceptance procedure, used in SOLAS 1974, MARPOL and the collision regulations. It reverses the default: an amendment to the technical annexes is deemed accepted on a specified date unless objections are received beforehand from an agreed number of Parties. For SOLAS 1974 an amendment is deemed accepted at the end of two years from communication to Contracting Governments, unless objected to by more than one-third of Contracting Governments, or by Governments whose combined fleets are not less than 50 per cent of world gross merchant tonnage. Amendments now enter into force typically within 18 to 24 months. Once in force internationally each flag State must still give the instrument effect domestically - in India through the Merchant Shipping Act and rules made under it - and it is that domestic instrument which is enforced against the ship.

blocks.h: Why this structure scores

blocks.p: The stem prints no limbs but makes four separate demands, and the commonest failure is to answer the first and drift. Following one instrument through its life from adoption to amendment answers all four in a single narrative, and putting the two named terms side by side in step 3 lets the contrast be drawn explicitly - which is what an explain the terms instruction is asking for.

blocks.h: Why the machinery looks so cumbersome

blocks.p: A treaty binds sovereign States, and no State can be bound without its own consent - that single constitutional fact generates the whole apparatus. Adoption cannot bind, because the conference does not speak for any government. Signature cannot ordinarily bind, because most constitutions require a legislature to act before the executive can commit. Hence the two-step route, the deposited instrument, the depositary who counts, and the threshold that has to be reached before anyone is obliged to do anything. Tacit acceptance is the one place where the system bends: consent is still required, but silence is treated as consent, and that inversion is what made a technical convention maintainable.

blocks.h: Why this matters to a Chief Engineer

blocks.p: It explains a situation seen constantly in practice: an amendment has been adopted, the industry press is full of it, class has issued guidance - and it does not yet apply to the ship. It also explains why a ship may be subject to a requirement her flag State has not ratified, through port State control and the no more favourable treatment principle, and why the certificate on the bulkhead is issued under national law rather than under the convention directly. The Net-Zero Framework in Q8 of this paper is a live illustration of an instrument stalled between approval and adoption.

blocks.h: Four words that are not synonyms

ul: Adoption - the text is settled. Nobody is bound.
Signature - intent indicated. Ordinarily still nobody is bound.
Ratification / acceptance / approval - a signatory State becomes bound on deposit. The three differ in domestic formality only.
Accession - a non-signatory State becomes bound on deposit, in one step.

blocks.p: And separately: entry into force of the convention is not entry into force for a particular State, which usually follows some months after that State deposits its own instrument.

blocks.h: Common mistakes

ul: Saying a convention is in force once adopted, or once signed.
Using ratification and accession as synonyms, or inventing a difference between ratification, acceptance and approval.
Giving only a number of States for a technical convention and omitting the tonnage percentage - the double condition is the point of that part of the question.
Describing tacit acceptance as the way a convention enters into force. It is the way an amendment does.
Forgetting that the flag State must still legislate domestically.
Confusing a reservation with a declaration, or asserting that reservations are freely available - many technical conventions restrict them.

blocks.h: Examiner traps

ul: 'State the provision and its importance' - two things. Most candidates state the provision and never say why it exists.
'For a convention of important technical nature' is a specific category, and the expected answer is the double condition with a real example. A general answer scores poorly here.
The two terms are printed as (i) and (ii) with no marks attached, which tempts candidates to treat them as an afterthought. They are a named, explicit demand and should be answered properly.

blocks.h: Likely oral follow-up

ul: An amendment was adopted last month. When does it apply to your ship?
Your flag State has not ratified a convention. Can a port State detain you under it?
Who is the depositary for IMO conventions, and what does the depositary actually do?
Why did the 1960 SOLAS amendments never enter into force?
How does a convention become enforceable law in India?

blocks.h: Memory framework

blocks.p: One instrument, six stages: ADOPT, CONSENT, TERMS, THRESHOLD, TONNAGE, AMEND. Two pairs of numbers carry the technical-convention part: SOLAS 25 and 50%, MARPOL 15 and 50%. One pair carries amendment: two years, one-third or 50%. And one sentence carries the distinction the question asks for: ratification is the second step for a State that signed; accession is the only step for a State that did not.

blocks.h: Regulation and source map

ul: Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties 1969 - Art 14(2) acceptance and approval; Art 15 accession.
SOLAS 1974 - final clauses on entry into force; Article VIII amendments and tacit acceptance.
MARPOL 73/78 - Article 15 and the 1978 Protocol's entry into force condition.
IMO Convention Article 38(e) - the functions under which committees act.
India - the Merchant Shipping Act and rules made under it as the domestic vehicle.

blocks.h: Uncertainty and source strength

blocks.p: MIW holds no licensed copy of SOLAS or MARPOL. The entry into force conditions and the tacit acceptance thresholds are cited from the IMO's own explanatory material - which quotes the SOLAS wording directly - and from convention summaries, rather than from the convention texts. Entry into force provisions are named by effect where the article number could not be confirmed, in preference to asserting a number that might be wrong. The Vienna Convention Articles 14(2) and 15 are likewise cited as quoted on the IMO's page rather than read in the Convention. None of this material is time-sensitive: the machinery has been stable for decades and the two worked examples are historical facts.

regulations: Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties 1969, Article 14(2)

quick_revision.recall_15s: Adoption is not entry into force. An IMO organ or a diplomatic conference adopts the text; that settles the wording and binds nobody. The text is then opened for signature and a State expresses consent to be bound in one of three ways: signature alone where the treaty allows it; signature subject to ratification, acceptance or approval, where signature is only an indication of intent and the State must later deposit a formal instrument - the interval being what lets it enact domestic legislation and satisfy constitutional requirements, with acceptance and approval being less formal equivalents of ratification under VCLT Article 14(2); and accession, a single step by which a State that did not sign within the signature period becomes a party by depositing an instrument of accession, under VCLT Article 15. All are deposited with the Secretary-General as depositary, who counts and notifies. The provision. Every convention carries a final clause fixing its entry into force - a threshold of acceptances plus a waiting period. It matters because it prevents an instrument binding only a handful of States, fixes the date obligations begin, and gives Administrations, class and owners time to prepare. Technical conventions use a double condition: a minimum number of States and a percentage of world merchant fleet gross tonnage - SOLAS 1974, 25 States and 50%, in force 25 May 1980; the 1978 MARPOL Protocol, 15 States and 50%, twelve months after. Tonnage ensures the major fleets are inside rather than a majority of small ones. Afterwards, amendment is by tacit acceptance: deemed accepted unless objected to - for SOLAS, at the end of two years from communication, unless more than one-third of Contracting Governments or Governments owning at least 50% of world gross merchant tonnage object. Amendments now enter into force in about 18 to 24 months; under the old explicit system, 1960 SOLAS amendments adopted between 1966 and 1973 never entered into force at all.
critical_numbers: SOLAS 1974: 25 States whose combined merchant fleets are not less than 50 per cent of world gross tonnage; adopted 1 November 1974, in force 25 May 1980
1978 MARPOL Protocol: 15 States and not less than 50 per cent of world gross tonnage, entering into force twelve months later

SOLAS tacit acceptance: deemed accepted at the end of two years from communication unless objected to by more than one-third of Contracting Governments, or Governments owning at least 50 per cent of world gross merchant tonnage
Amendments now enter into force in about 18 to 24 months
quick_revision.critical_regulation: The final clauses of each convention - SOLAS 1974 and the 1978 MARPOL Protocol - read with the tacit acceptance procedure in SOLAS Article VIII; Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties Articles 14(2) and 15.
quick_revision.major_trap: Treating adoption, signature and entry into force as one event, or using ratification and accession as synonyms. Signature subject to ratification is a two-step route for a State that was present and signed; accession is a one-step route for a State that was not, or that did not sign in time. The effect once the instrument is deposited is the same - the difference is the path, not the result. The second trap is conflating the entry into force of the convention with the entry into force of an amendment: they use different thresholds and different procedures.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Give the route for the entry into force question.
retrieval_cards.answer: 1 Adoption is not entry into force. 2 How consent to be bound is expressed. 3 The two named terms. 4 The entry into force provision and why it matters. 5 Technical conventions and the double condition. 6 Tacit acceptance afterwards.
retrieval_cards.why: The paper makes four demands in one undivided stem; this order answers them all and puts the named terms where they can be contrasted.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Explain accession.
retrieval_cards.answer: The means by which a State becomes party to a treaty it did not sign during the signature period. It is a single act - depositing an instrument of accession with the depositary - with no prior signature, and it has the same legal effect as ratification. Vienna Convention Article 15 permits it where the treaty so provides.
retrieval_cards.why: One step versus two is the whole distinction, and the question asks for both terms so they must be contrastable.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Explain signature subject to ratification, acceptance or approval.
retrieval_cards.answer: The State signs to indicate intent, but signature does not bind it. It becomes bound only when it later deposits a formal instrument of ratification, acceptance or approval. The interval allows it to enact the domestic legislation and satisfy the constitutional requirements needed to give effect to the treaty.
retrieval_cards.why: The reason for the two-step route - domestic legislation - is the part that earns the mark.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What is the difference between ratification, acceptance and approval?
retrieval_cards.answer: None in legal effect. Acceptance and approval are less formal alternatives to ratification, used where a State's constitution does not require the fuller procedure. Vienna Convention Article 14(2) provides that consent is expressed by acceptance or approval under conditions similar to those applying to ratification.
retrieval_cards.why: Candidates invent distinctions between these three. There are none in effect, and saying so is the correct answer.

retrieval_cards.prompt: State the entry into force conditions for SOLAS 1974 and for the 1978 MARPOL Protocol.
retrieval_cards.answer: SOLAS 1974 required acceptance by not less than 25 States whose combined merchant fleets constitute not less than 50 per cent of world merchant shipping gross tonnage; it was adopted on 1 November 1974 and entered into force on 25 May 1980. The 1978 MARPOL Protocol required 15 States and not less than 50 per cent of world gross tonnage, entering into force twelve months afterwards.
retrieval_cards.why: The question asks specifically about conventions of an important technical nature, and these are the two worked examples every candidate should hold.

retrieval_cards.prompt: How does the tacit acceptance procedure work for a SOLAS amendment?
retrieval_cards.answer: The amendment is deemed to have been accepted at the end of two years from the date it is communicated to Contracting Governments, unless it is objected to by more than one-third of Contracting Governments, or by Contracting Governments owning at least 50 per cent of world gross merchant tonnage. It then enters into force on a specified date.
retrieval_cards.why: It reverses the default from opt-in to opt-out, which is why amendments now take 18 to 24 months instead of never.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Why is a percentage of world tonnage used as well as a number of States?
retrieval_cards.answer: Because a number of States alone could be satisfied by many small flags while the major fleets stayed outside, leaving the convention technically in force but commercially irrelevant. The tonnage criterion ensures the ships that matter are actually covered.
retrieval_cards.why: The examiner asks for the importance of the provision, and this is the reasoning behind the double condition.

questions.understand_first: The single idea behind this question is that agreeing the words and being bound by them are two separate events, often years apart. A conference settles the text - that is adoption, and at that moment the convention binds nobody at all. Each State then decides separately whether to take it on, and the treaty itself specifies how many must do so, and how much of the world's shipping they must represent, before it becomes law for anyone. That second condition is why a technical convention carries a tonnage threshold: a safety rule in force only among States that own no ships would achieve nothing. The two terms named in the question are simply two routes to the same destination - one where a State signs first and confirms later, once its parliament has passed the legislation it needs, and one where it never signed at all and joins afterwards in a single step. And because the gap between adoption and force can run to a decade, conventions carry a faster machinery for amending themselves.

blocks.h: 1. What the revised strategy is, and what it is not

blocks.p: The 2023 IMO Strategy on Reduction of GHG Emissions from Ships was adopted by resolution MEPC.377(80) on 7 July 2023 at MEPC 80, replacing the Initial Strategy of 2018. Its vision commits the Organization to reducing GHG emissions from international shipping and, as a matter of urgency, phasing them out as soon as possible, while promoting a just and equitable transition.

It is essential to be clear what the Strategy is: an adopted policy resolution stating intent, ambitions and candidate measures. It is not mandatory law and binds no ship. Obligations arise only when measures are written into MARPOL Annex VI.

blocks.h: 2. The four levels of ambition

ol: Carbon intensity of the ship to decline - review with the aim of strengthening the energy efficiency design requirements for new ships;
carbon intensity of international shipping to decline - reduce CO2 per transport work, as an average across international shipping, by at least 40% by 2030, compared to 2008;
uptake of zero or near-zero GHG technologies, fuels and/or energy sources to increase - to at least 5%, striving for 10%, of the energy used by international shipping by 2030;

GHG emissions to reach net zero - peak as soon as possible and reach net-zero by or around, i.e. close to, 2050, taking account of different national circumstances, consistent with the Paris Agreement temperature goal.

blocks.p: The ambitions are assessed well-to-wake under the LCA guidelines (resolution MEPC.376(80)), so emissions cannot simply be shifted from the funnel to the fuel production chain.

blocks.h: 3. The indicative checkpoints and the guiding principles

blocks.p: Two indicative checkpoints are added, expressed - unlike the ambitions - in total annual GHG emissions: reduce them by at least 20%, striving for 30%, by 2030, and by at least 70%, striving for 80%, by 2040, both compared to 2008.

The guiding principles include non-discrimination and no more favourable treatment as enshrined in MARPOL; common but differentiated responsibilities and respective capabilities in the light of different national circumstances; effect to be given by all ships regardless of flag; and consideration of impacts on States, particularly LDCs and SIDS. The tension between the second and third is precisely what later stalled adoption.

blocks.h: 4. The basket of measures - technical and economic

blocks.p: Short-term measures are already in force under Annex VI - EEXI, the CII under regulation 28, and the SEEMP. For the mid-term the Strategy identifies a basket of two complementary elements: a technical element, a goal-based marine fuel standard phasing down the GHG intensity of marine fuel; and an economic element, a maritime GHG emissions pricing mechanism. The two were to be delivered as a single instrument, the standard setting the trajectory and the price making non-compliance dearer than compliance.

blocks.h: 5. The proposed new Chapter 5 - the Net-Zero Framework

blocks.p: That instrument was finalised as the IMO Net-Zero Framework and approved at MEPC 83 in April 2025 as amendments introducing a new Chapter 5, Regulations on the IMO Net-Zero Framework. As approved in draft it would:

ul: apply to ships over 5,000 gross tonnage, about 85% of international shipping's CO2;
require an annual GHG Fuel Intensity (GFI) in gCO2eq/MJ, well-to-wake, against a 2008 reference of 93.3, with zero or near-zero fuels at not more than 19.0;
set two tiers - a Base Target and a stricter Direct Compliance Target - at 4% and 17% for 2028, 8% and 21% for 2030 and 30% and 43% for 2035;
require a ship falling short to buy remedial units at USD 100 per tonne CO2eq (Tier 1) and USD 380 (Tier 2), the higher tier penalising the most carbon-intensive fuels;
allow ships beating the Direct Compliance Target to earn surplus units, transferable, bankable for up to two years, or cancellable;

direct contributions to an IMO Net-Zero Fund rewarding low-emission ships and supporting innovation, training and technology transfer in developing countries - the mechanism through which the just-transition principle would operate.

blocks.p: The first reporting period was to begin on 1 January 2028.

blocks.h: 6. Where the amendments actually stood at this sitting

blocks.p: Here an answer must be accurate rather than optimistic. A second extraordinary session of the MEPC met from 14 to 17 October 2025 specifically to adopt the draft amendments. Consensus could not be reached. The principal points of contention were the acceptance procedure - tacit versus explicit, a proposed clause recognising the Framework as the sole global mid-term measure, and concerns over overlap with regional regimes, compliance cost and administrative burden on developing States.

On 17 October 2025 the Committee agreed to adjourn the session for one year, Member States continuing to work towards consensus meanwhile. At the date of this examination the amendments were therefore approved but neither adopted nor in force, and no entry-into-force date existed. If subsequently adopted under tacit acceptance, entry into force would follow about 16 months later.

The position is best summarised thus: the Strategy is adopted policy; the short-term measures are in force; the mid-term measures remain draft law awaiting agreement. The design is settled; adoption is a political question, not a technical one.

blocks.h: Why this structure scores

blocks.p: The stem contains two demands and no limbs, so the risk is an undifferentiated essay. Steps 1 to 3 discharge the Strategy, step 4 is the hinge that explains why Chapter 5 exists at all, and steps 5 to 6 discharge the amendments. Step 6 is what makes the answer worth full marks in February 2026: an otherwise excellent answer that assumes the framework is law has failed on the one fact the examiner's own wording - amendments being considered - shows he knew.

blocks.h: The examiner's wording is a dated fingerprint

blocks.p: Read the stem again: amendments being considered under MARPOL Annex VI, including the inclusion of new Chapter-V. That is not loose drafting. It is an accurate description of the position in February 2026 and it tells you the paper was set with the October 2025 outcome in view. When an examiner's own words describe an instrument as under consideration, an answer that describes it as in force contradicts the question.

blocks.h: Strategy, approval, adoption, entry into force

blocks.p: This question is the live illustration of the machinery examined in Q7 of this same paper, and the two should be revised together. The sequence is: a strategy states intent; a committee approves a draft text; a session adopts it, which is what makes it an amendment to the convention; and it then enters into force, ordinarily by tacit acceptance after a stated period. The Net-Zero Framework reached stage two and stalled between stages two and three. That is why the dispute at ES.2 over tacit versus explicit acceptance was not a procedural quibble: tacit acceptance would bind objecting States unless enough of them formally objected, and explicit acceptance would not, so the choice determines whether a State can stay outside.

blocks.h: Why consensus failed, in substance

ul: The principles collide. No more favourable treatment and all ships regardless of flag demand a uniform global measure. Common but differentiated responsibilities demands that developing States not bear equal burden. A single carbon price applied to every ship is hard to reconcile with both.

Regional overlap. The EU had already brought shipping into its Emissions Trading System and adopted FuelEU Maritime. A clause declaring the IMO framework the sole global mid-term measure was an attempt to force regional schemes to give way, and was resisted.
Cost and burden. Remedial unit prices of USD 100 and USD 380 per tonne CO2eq are a material operating cost, and several delegations doubted the administrative machinery could be built by 2028.

blocks.h: Common mistakes

ul: Stating that the Net-Zero Framework was adopted in October 2025, or that it enters into force in 2027. Neither is true; both appear widely in material written before October 2025.
Treating the 2023 Strategy as mandatory. It is a policy resolution.
Mixing the levels of ambition with the indicative checkpoints - intensity and fuel uptake against total annual emissions.
Dropping the striving for figures, which are part of the adopted wording.
Omitting the 2008 baseline, without which every percentage is meaningless.
Forgetting the well-to-wake basis, which is what stops emissions being exported upstream.
Confusing GFI with CII. GFI is the carbon intensity of the fuel; CII is the operational carbon intensity of the ship.

quick_revision.recall_15s: The Strategy. Resolution MEPC.377(80), adopted 7 July 2023 at MEPC 80, replacing the Initial Strategy of 2018. It is a policy framework, not mandatory law. Four levels of ambition: strengthen energy efficiency design requirements for new ships; reduce CO2 per transport work by at least 40% by 2030 against 2008; zero or near-zero technologies, fuels and energy sources to be at least 5%, striving for 10%, of energy used by 2030; and peak GHG as soon as possible, reaching net-zero by or around, close to, 2050. Two indicative checkpoints on total annual GHG against 2008: at least 20%, striving for 30%, by 2030, and at least 70%, striving for 80%, by 2040. Measured well-to-wake under the LCA guidelines, MEPC.376(80). Guiding principles include no more favourable treatment, effect regardless of flag, common but differentiated responsibilities, and impacts on LDCs and SIDS. The measures. Short-term measures - EEXI, CII, SEEMP - are already in force. The mid-term basket has a technical element, a goal-based marine fuel standard, and an economic element, a GHG pricing mechanism. Together they became the Net-Zero Framework, approved at MEPC 83 in April 2025 as a new Chapter 5 of MARPOL Annex VI for ships over 5,000 GT: GHG Fuel Intensity in gCO2eq/MJ against a 2008 reference of 93.3, zero or near-zero at 19.0 or less, a Base Target and a stricter Direct Compliance Target (4% and 17% in 2028, 8% and 21% in 2030, 30% and 43% in 2035), remedial units at USD 100 and USD 380 per tonne CO2eq, tradeable and bankable surplus units, and an IMO Net-Zero Fund. Status at this sitting. The extraordinary session convened to adopt them, 14 to 17 October 2025, could not reach consensus and was ADJOURNED for twelve months. Chapter 5 was therefore approved but not adopted and not in force.

quick_revision.major_trap: Writing as though the Net-Zero Framework were law. At the date of this examination the draft Chapter 5 had been approved but not adopted: the extraordinary session convened to adopt it in October 2025 was adjourned for twelve months without agreement, so nothing was in force and no entry-into-force date existed. Much material written between April and October 2025 states that the framework would be adopted in October 2025 and enter into force in 2027, and repeating that is the single biggest error available in this question. The related trap is treating the 2023 Strategy itself as mandatory - it is a policy resolution.

questions.understand_first: Two things in this question are at completely different points in their legal lives, and the whole answer turns on keeping them apart. The 2023 Strategy is an adopted IMO resolution, but it is policy - it states what the Organization intends and binds nobody. The new Chapter 5 would be mandatory law under MARPOL Annex VI - and at the date of this examination it had been approved in draft but not adopted, because the session convened to adopt it in October 2025 adjourned for a year without agreement. So every target in the Strategy is real but aspirational, and every figure in Chapter 5 is precise but provisional.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Give the route for the GHG strategy and Chapter 5 question.
retrieval_cards.answer: 1 What the revised strategy is and is not. 2 The four levels of ambition. 3 Checkpoints and guiding principles. 4 The basket of measures. 5 The proposed new Chapter 5. 6 Where the amendments actually stood.
retrieval_cards.why: Steps 1 to 3 are the strategy, 4 is the bridge, 5 to 6 the amendments - and step 6 is what separates a current answer from a stale one.

retrieval_cards.prompt: State the four levels of ambition of the 2023 IMO GHG Strategy.
retrieval_cards.answer: Strengthen energy efficiency design requirements for new ships; reduce CO2 emissions per transport work across international shipping by at least 40% by 2030 compared to 2008; zero or near-zero GHG technologies, fuels and energy sources to represent at least 5%, striving for 10%, of energy used by 2030; and peak GHG emissions as soon as possible, reaching net-zero by or around, close to, 2050.
retrieval_cards.why: Resolution MEPC.377(80) paragraph 3.3. The striving-for figures are part of the wording and are routinely dropped.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What is the difference between the levels of ambition and the indicative checkpoints?
retrieval_cards.answer: The levels of ambition concern carbon intensity and the uptake of zero or near-zero fuels. The indicative checkpoints concern total annual GHG emissions from international shipping - at least 20% striving for 30% by 2030, and at least 70% striving for 80% by 2040, both against 2008.
retrieval_cards.why: Two different sets of numbers measuring two different things, and mixing them is the commonest factual error in this topic.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What was the legal status of the new MARPOL Annex VI Chapter 5 at the February 2026 sitting?
retrieval_cards.answer: Approved but not adopted, and not in force. MEPC 83 approved the draft in April 2025, but the extraordinary session convened to adopt it from 14 to 17 October 2025 could not reach consensus and was adjourned for twelve months. No entry-into-force date existed.
retrieval_cards.why: This is the highest-value fact in the paper. Sources written before October 2025 confidently predict adoption and a 2027 entry into force, and repeating them is wrong.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What are the two elements of the proposed Net-Zero Framework?
retrieval_cards.answer: A global fuel standard requiring a ship's annual GHG Fuel Intensity, measured well-to-wake in gCO2eq/MJ, to fall against a 2008 reference of 93.3; and a pricing mechanism under which a shortfall is met by purchasing remedial units, with contributions going to an IMO Net-Zero Fund.
retrieval_cards.why: This is the technical-plus-economic basket of the 2023 Strategy turned into a single instrument.

retrieval_cards.prompt: In the draft framework, what were the two compliance tiers and the remedial unit prices?
retrieval_cards.answer: A Base Target and a stricter Direct Compliance Target - 4% and 17% for 2028, 8% and 21% for 2030, 30% and 43% for 2035. Remedial units were priced at USD 100 per tonne CO2eq for Tier 1 and USD 380 for Tier 2. These are draft figures from a text that was not adopted.
retrieval_cards.why: Precise but provisional. Quote them with that qualification, never as law.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Why did the October 2025 extraordinary session fail to adopt the framework?
retrieval_cards.answer: Consensus could not be reached. The main points of contention were the acceptance procedure - tacit versus explicit - a clause recognising the framework as the sole global mid-term measure, and concerns about overlap with regional regimes, compliance cost and administrative burden, particularly their impact on developing States.
retrieval_cards.why: The reasons show why the outcome was a deferral rather than a rejection, and they connect to the Strategy's own guiding principles.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Which resolution is the 2023 IMO GHG Strategy, and when was it adopted?
retrieval_cards.answer: Resolution MEPC.377(80), adopted on 7 July 2023 at the eightieth session of the Marine Environment Protection Committee. It replaced the Initial IMO Strategy of 2018.
retrieval_cards.why: A resolution number and date convert a general essay into a cited answer.

blocks.h: 1. a) The zones, and what the coastal State holds in each

blocks.p: UNCLOS measures zones from the baselines, and the coastal State's authority thins progressively seaward - from full sovereignty to defined functional rights and finally to none.

ul: Internal waters - landward of the baselines. Full sovereignty, with no right of innocent passage.
Territorial sea, up to 12 n.m. - sovereignty, extending to airspace, seabed and subsoil, subject to innocent passage.
Contiguous zone, to 24 n.m. - not sovereignty but control, to prevent and punish infringement of customs, fiscal, immigration and sanitary laws.
Exclusive Economic Zone, to 200 n.m. - sovereign rights, not sovereignty.
Continental shelf - sovereign rights over seabed and subsoil, existing independently of occupation or proclamation.
High seas - no State may validly claim sovereignty; the high seas freedoms apply.

blocks.h: 2. What the coastal State may actually do

ul: Territorial sea - full prescriptive and enforcement jurisdiction; its criminal and civil law applies. It may legislate on navigation, cables, fishing, pollution and customs, but must not hamper innocent passage, which ceases to be innocent on acts prejudicial to peace, good order or security.
Contiguous zone - powers confined to those four subjects, preventive and punitive only.

EEZ - Article 56 gives sovereign rights for exploring, exploiting, conserving and managing the natural resources, plus jurisdiction over artificial islands and installations, marine scientific research and protection of the marine environment. Article 73 permits boarding, inspection and arrest for fisheries offences.
The limit is the point: outside those purposes the coastal State has no general jurisdiction in the EEZ. It is not territory.

blocks.h: 3. The flag State - nationality, freedoms and exclusive jurisdiction

ul: Article 91 - each State fixes the conditions for granting nationality and registration; a genuine link must exist.
Article 92 - a ship sails under one flag only and is subject to the flag State's exclusive jurisdiction on the high seas.

Article 94 - the flag State must effectively exercise jurisdiction and control in administrative, technical and social matters - construction, equipment, seaworthiness, manning, labour conditions, training - and hold an inquiry into serious casualties.

Article 58 - in the EEZ all States retain the freedoms of navigation and overflight, and Articles 88 to 115, including Article 92, apply so far as not incompatible. The flag State's authority therefore travels with the ship into the EEZ.

blocks.h: 4. How the two are reconciled - due regard

blocks.p: UNCLOS resolves the overlap by a reciprocal standard, not a hierarchy: the coastal State exercises its EEZ rights with due regard to other States' rights, and other States exercise their freedoms with due regard to the coastal State's, complying with its laws made in conformity with the Convention. Residual rights are resolved on equity and all relevant circumstances. Across every zone, Article 98 obliges every master to render assistance to any person in danger of being lost at sea.

blocks.h: 5. b) The missing cadet - which law applies

blocks.p: The tempting answer is that Indian law applies because the ship was in India's EEZ. That is wrong. The EEZ is not Indian territory; India's authority there is functional - resources, installations, research, the marine environment - and a person missing from a ship engages none of it. Because Article 58 carries Article 92 into the EEZ, shipboard matters remain under the exclusive jurisdiction of the flag State. The determining question is whose flag the vessel flies.

ul: Indian-flagged - Indian law applies in full through the flag. Under the Merchant Shipping Act 1958: s.358, loss of life by reason of a casualty on board is a shipping casualty, the master giving immediate notice to the officer appointed by the Central Government; s.359, that officer reports in writing and may hold a preliminary inquiry; s.452, the proper officer inquires into the cause of death, endorses the official log book as to whether the stated cause is true, and if death appears caused by violence or other improper means reports to the Director-General. Indian criminal law reaches the ship through s.1(5) of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita 2023 - any offence on a ship registered in India wherever it may be.

Foreign-flagged - the flag State's law governs the investigation and any prosecution, and its Administration conducts the casualty investigation. India acts as coastal State and, decisively, as the State responsible for search and rescue in its search and rescue region - a duty owed regardless of flag under Article 98 and the SAR Convention. India may also be a substantially interested State if the cadet was an Indian national.

blocks.h: 6. The actions to be taken

ol: Immediate. Raise the man overboard alarm and mark the position; muster and account for every person on board to establish who is missing and when last seen, since the search datum must be reconstructed. Commence a search, return along the track, post lookouts, and broadcast to the MRCC and ships in the vicinity.
Preserve. Secure the cabin and last known location; preserve CCTV, gangway and access records, rest-hour records and personal effects; take statements early; make full official log book entries.
Notify. Owner and manager, the DPA, the flag State, the coordinating coastal State authority, the P&I club, the manning agent, and - through the company - the next of kin.

Report and investigate. Loss of life makes this a very serious marine casualty, so a safety investigation follows under the Casualty Investigation Code alongside the flag State's inquiry; for an Indian ship the s.358 notice and s.359 report apply.

Company review and welfare. Treat it under the ISM Code as an accident and non-conformity - safety of access, work overside, lifebuoy provision, fatigue, and bullying, harassment and isolation examined honestly - and discharge MLC 2006 obligations on repatriation of remains, compensation for death and support to dependants, while supporting the remaining crew.

blocks.h: Why this structure scores

blocks.p: Limb (a) asks about both States and most answers describe only the coastal one. Splitting the limb into coastal State, flag State and the due-regard reconciliation guarantees that the flag half is present, and it sets up limb (b), which cannot be answered without it. Limb (b) is only 6 marks but it contains the single highest-value insight in the question, so it should be led with the jurisdictional point and not with a list of actions.

blocks.h: Why the EEZ is the way it is

blocks.p: The EEZ was the great compromise of UNCLOS III. Coastal States - especially newly independent ones - wanted the fish and the oil off their coasts; maritime States wanted their ships and aircraft to keep moving. The zone gives each side what it actually needed: economic control to the coastal State and navigational freedom to everyone else. Understanding that bargain tells you immediately what the coastal State can and cannot do, without memorising a list: if the issue is a resource, an installation, research or pollution, it is the coastal State's; if it is about the ship as a ship - her navigation, her crew, her internal affairs - it remains the flag State's.

blocks.h: Sovereignty, sovereign rights, jurisdiction - three different words

ul: Sovereignty - the full authority of a State over its territory. Internal waters and territorial sea.
Sovereign rights - exclusive rights for a defined purpose. The EEZ and continental shelf. Exclusive, but purposive.
Jurisdiction - the power to prescribe and enforce law over specified subject matter, such as artificial islands or marine scientific research in the EEZ.

blocks.p: The question uses the phrase sovereign rights and jurisdictions deliberately, and an answer that treats the three as interchangeable has missed what is being tested.

blocks.h: Missing is not the same as dead

blocks.p: The scenario says the cadet goes missing, not that he was seen to fall or that a body was recovered, and that distinction has practical and legal consequences. Practically, the search datum must be reconstructed from the last confirmed sighting rather than from a position, which is why the muster is the critical first step and why gangway records and CCTV matter so much. Legally, a presumption of death normally requires a formal process and takes time, which affects wages, the seafarer employment agreement, insurance, and the family's ability to deal with the estate. A candidate who writes as though a death certificate follows automatically has misunderstood the situation the crew is actually in.

blocks.h: Common mistakes

ul: Assuming Indian law applies because the incident was in India's EEZ. It is not territory.
Forgetting to ask what flag the ship flies - the question does not say, and that omission is the test.
Describing only the coastal State's rights in limb (a) and ignoring the flag State.
Saying the coastal State has sovereignty in the EEZ, or that it has no rights at all there. Neither is right.
Citing the Indian Penal Code, replaced by the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita 2023 on 1 July 2024.
Treating search and rescue as depending on jurisdiction. It does not - Article 98 and the SAR Convention apply regardless of flag.

blocks.h: Memory framework

blocks.p: Sail outward and watch authority thin: internal (all) - territorial 12 (all, but passage) - contiguous 24 (four subjects) - EEZ 200 (resources only) - shelf (seabed) - high seas (none). Then remember the flag State's authority is constant across all of them, which is why limb (b) resolves as it does. For the incident: WHOSE FLAG, then SEARCH, SECURE, REPORT, INQUIRE, SUPPORT.

blocks.h: Regulation and source map

ul: UNCLOS - Art 2 and 3 territorial sea; Art 17 to 19 innocent passage; Art 33 contiguous zone; Art 56 EEZ sovereign rights; Art 58 freedoms and application of the high seas articles; Art 73 enforcement; Art 76 continental shelf; Art 87 high seas freedoms; Art 91 nationality and genuine link; Art 92 exclusive flag State jurisdiction; Art 94 flag State duties; Art 98 duty to render assistance.
India - Maritime Zones Act 1976 declaring the zones; Merchant Shipping Act 1958 s.358, s.359 and s.452; Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita 2023 s.1(5).

blocks.h: Uncertainty, jurisdiction and currency

blocks.p: MIW holds no licensed copy of UNCLOS, so the zone limits and Articles 56, 58 and 92 are cited from academic and institutional commentary rather than from the Convention text; the propositions are uncontroversial and consistently reported, and the article numbering is flagged for confirmation before being relied on. India's Maritime Zones Act 1976 was not read in the statute and no section is asserted. The description of India's national search and rescue machinery is given in functional terms - who coordinates and through what kind of centre - rather than by citing an instrument, because the designating instrument was not verified. Two currency points matter. First, the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita 2023 replaced the Indian Penal Code on 1 July 2024, so any answer citing the IPC is out of date - the same class of error as the superseded-edition problems recorded elsewhere in this series. Second, as with Q5, the Merchant Shipping Act 1958 was in force at this sitting and was repealed by the Merchant Shipping Act 2025 with effect from 15 March 2026; the answer is given at the sitting date and the corresponding provisions of the 2025 Act must be confirmed before being relied on.

questions.short_title: UNCLOS Maritime Zones and a Missing Cadet in the EEZ
regulations: UNCLOS Articles 2, 3, 17-19 (territorial sea and innocent passage)
UNCLOS Articles 87, 91, 92, 94 (high seas, nationality, flag State duties)

quick_revision.recall_15s: (a) Zones outward: internal waters, full sovereignty; territorial sea up to 12 n.m., sovereignty extending to airspace, seabed and subsoil, but subject to innocent passage; contiguous zone to 24 n.m., where the coastal State has control - not sovereignty - to prevent and punish infringement of customs, fiscal, immigration and sanitary laws; EEZ to 200 n.m., where under Article 56 the coastal State has sovereign rights for exploring, exploiting, conserving and managing natural resources, living and non-living, plus jurisdiction over artificial islands, marine scientific research and protection of the marine environment; continental shelf, sovereign rights over seabed and subsoil; and the high seas, where no State may claim sovereignty. Sovereignty thins into functional rights as you go out. The flag State grants nationality with a genuine link (Art 91), has exclusive jurisdiction over its ships on the high seas (Art 92), and owes duties on administrative, technical and social matters (Art 94). Under Article 58, freedom of navigation continues in the EEZ and the high seas articles apply so far as compatible. Both sides owe due regard to the other, and every master owes the Article 98 duty to render assistance. (b) The EEZ is not Indian territory, so the law that applies to what happens on board follows the flag. If the ship is Indian-flagged: the Merchant Shipping Act 1958 applies - s.358 shipping casualty including loss of life, s.359 report and preliminary inquiry, s.452 inquiry into cause of death with an official log endorsement and a report to the Director-General if death was by violence or improper means - and Indian criminal law applies through BNS 2023 s.1(5), which reaches any offence on a ship registered in India wherever she may be. If she is foreign-flagged, the flag State's law governs the investigation and any prosecution, and India acts as coastal State only for search and rescue within its search and rescue region. Actions: raise man overboard, muster and account for all hands, search and broadcast to the MRCC, preserve the scene and records, notify owner, DPA, flag State, P&I and next of kin, treat it as a very serious marine casualty for investigation, make the official log entries, and discharge the MLC obligations on repatriation of remains and compensation.

MSA 1958 s.358 shipping casualties; s.359 report to Central Government; s.452 inquiry into cause of death on an Indian ship

quick_revision.major_trap: Assuming that because the incident occurred in India's Exclusive Economic Zone, Indian law applies. The EEZ is not territory: India's rights there are functional and concern resources, artificial islands, research and the marine environment, none of which reaches a person missing from a ship. What happens on board follows the flag. India's search and rescue responsibility is a separate duty and does apply regardless of flag. A second trap is citing the Indian Penal Code, which was replaced by the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita 2023 with effect from 1 July 2024.

questions.understand_first: The phrase in the Exclusive Economic Zone of India tempts everyone into the same error. The EEZ is not Indian territory. India holds only functional rights there - over resources, artificial islands, research and the marine environment - and nothing in that list covers a person going missing from a ship. What happens on board a ship is an internal matter of the ship, and internal matters follow the flag. So the first question is never 'where did it happen', but 'whose flag is she flying' - and only then does India's role become clear: search and rescue always, because that is a duty owed to everyone, but investigation and prosecution only if she is Indian.
questions.memory_cue: Limb (a) sails outward: INTERNAL - TERRITORIAL - CONTIGUOUS - EEZ - SHELF - HIGH SEAS (1), with rights thinning as you go (2), then the flag State's constant authority (3) and due regard where they meet (4). Limb (b): WHOSE FLAG (5), then SEARCH - SECURE - REPORT - INQUIRE (6). Limits 12, 24, 200.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Give the route for the UNCLOS zones and missing cadet question.
retrieval_cards.answer: 1 The zones and what the coastal State holds in each. 2 What the coastal State may actually do. 3 The flag State - nationality, freedoms and exclusive jurisdiction. 4 Due regard. 5 The missing cadet - which law applies. 6 The actions to be taken.
retrieval_cards.why: Steps 1 to 4 are the 10-mark limb, steps 5 and 6 the 6-mark limb.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What is the difference between sovereignty in the territorial sea and sovereign rights in the EEZ?
retrieval_cards.answer: In the territorial sea the coastal State has full sovereignty, subject only to innocent passage, so its laws apply generally. In the EEZ it has only sovereign rights for a defined purpose - exploring, exploiting, conserving and managing natural resources - plus jurisdiction over artificial islands, marine scientific research and the marine environment. It is functional authority, not territory.
retrieval_cards.why: This single distinction decides limb (b) and is the highest-value sentence in the question.

retrieval_cards.prompt: State the outer limits of the territorial sea, contiguous zone and EEZ.
retrieval_cards.answer: Territorial sea up to 12 nautical miles from the baselines; contiguous zone up to 24 nautical miles; exclusive economic zone up to 200 nautical miles.
retrieval_cards.why: Three numbers that anchor the whole of limb (a).

retrieval_cards.prompt: What does UNCLOS Article 92 provide, and does it help in the EEZ?
retrieval_cards.answer: That ships are subject to the exclusive jurisdiction of the flag State on the high seas. It matters in the EEZ because Article 58 applies the high seas articles to the EEZ so far as they are not incompatible with the EEZ regime, so shipboard matters continue to follow the flag.
retrieval_cards.why: This is the chain of reasoning that takes you from a scenario set in the EEZ to the flag State's law.

retrieval_cards.prompt: A cadet goes missing in India's EEZ. Does Indian law automatically apply?
retrieval_cards.answer: No. The EEZ is not Indian territory and India's rights there do not extend to internal shipboard matters. If the ship is Indian-flagged, Indian law applies through the flag. If she is foreign-flagged, the flag State's law governs investigation and prosecution, though India retains search and rescue responsibility within its search and rescue region.
retrieval_cards.why: The question deliberately does not state the flag, and identifying that gap is what the examiner is testing.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Which Indian merchant shipping provisions bite if the ship is Indian-flagged and a person is lost?
retrieval_cards.answer: MSA 1958 section 358, under which loss of life by reason of a casualty on board is a shipping casualty and the master must give immediate notice; section 359, under which the officer reports to the Central Government and may hold a preliminary inquiry; and section 452, under which the proper officer inquires into the cause of death, endorses the official log book, and reports to the Director-General if death appears to have been caused by violence or other improper means.
retrieval_cards.why: Three named sections turn a general answer about procedure into a legal one.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Which Indian penal statute reaches an offence committed on board an Indian ship, and since when?
retrieval_cards.answer: The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita 2023, section 1(5), which applies to any offence committed by any person on any ship or aircraft registered in India wherever it may be. It came into force on 1 July 2024, replacing the Indian Penal Code 1860.
retrieval_cards.why: Citing the IPC is a currency error after July 2024 and is exactly the sort of superseded-instrument trap this series keeps producing.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What are the master's immediate actions when a person is found missing at sea?
retrieval_cards.answer: Raise the man overboard alarm and mark the position, muster and account for every person on board to confirm who is missing and when last seen, commence a search and initiate a return to the search datum, broadcast to the MRCC and to ships in the vicinity, and preserve the scene, CCTV and records while the search continues.
retrieval_cards.why: Missing is not the same as seen to fall - accounting for all hands is what establishes the datum, and it is the step most often omitted.
